#4400. European Union Cracks Down on Predatory Gaming Practices

Modern games have found plenty of ways to make a small purchase more complicated than it should be. You buy in-game currency instead of the item you want, spend that currency on a random reward, and sometimes end up with just enough left over to tempt another top-up.

The studio is giving Kiln, its pottery-themed multiplayer game, another shot.

Now, the European Commission wants to put limits on some of these practices. On November 11, it unveiled the proposed Digital Fairness Act, a set of consumer-protection rules covering loot boxes, premium currencies, subscription traps, and manipulative design, and although games aren't its only target, they're very much part of it.

Under the proposal, games could no longer sell paid loot boxes to minors. Adults would still be allowed to buy them, but publishers would have to show the possible rewards and their odds, and give players an accessible way to turn the system off.

Pay-to-win and pay-to-progress mechanics would also be prohibited for minors. That second term is important because it could cover purchases that let players skip a grind, not just items that give them an advantage over someone else. Where the law draws that line will matter to publishers whose games rely on paid progression boosts.

Premium currencies are another target. Games would have to show what an in-game purchase costs in real money. Players shouldn't have to do the math just to find out what an item costs. Paid virtual currencies would also be switched off by default for minors unless a parent or guardian approves them.

Brazil passed a law against loot boxes for children last year, but the EU proposal covers more ground. It also doesn't mean adults are about to lose access to every microtransaction.

Outside gaming, the proposal targets "dark patterns" – misleading prompts and interfaces designed to push people into choices they didn't intend to make. That includes fake urgency, confusing options, and other tricks meant to keep people spending.

Subscriptions would get stricter rules, too. A free trial could only become a paid subscription with explicit consent, and canceling online should be straightforward. The Commission also wants renewal reminders instead of leaving customers to discover another charge after it's happened.

Players shouldn't have to do the math just to find out what an item costs.

Another part deals with addictive design. Businesses would have to let users disable certain features that encourage excessive use, such as unwanted notifications, autoplay, and streak rewards. The proposal also calls for clearer influencer advertising and tighter limits on personalized ads and prices aimed at minors.The Commission also highlights the difficulty of reaching a human customer-service representative. Earlier this month, a Battlefield 6 player won a court case against EA after an unexplained ban and unsuccessful attempts to appeal. That's a separate dispute, but the frustration of getting nowhere with support will sound familiar to plenty of players.

The gaming industry has already objected. In a joint statement, Video Games Europe and the European Games Developer Federation described the proposal as 'unworkable, unjustified and disproportionate.' They argue it could hurt European studios, particularly smaller ones, and leave players with fewer games to choose from.

The groups say the rules around in-game currencies are too broad and don't account for existing safeguards. They point to PEGI ratings, parental controls, and spending restrictions, and warn that the proposal could create more legal uncertainty. The industry groups have also suggested smaller currency top-ups and refunds for unused currency as alternatives.

The definitions of pay-to-win and pay-to-progress will be worth watching. They sound straightforward until you apply them to a game where almost everything can be earned through play or bought to save time.

For now, the Act is only a proposal. It still needs to go through the European Parliament and Council, where parts of it could change. No publisher is being ordered to pull loot boxes from its games today.

The Commission has separately proposed stronger consumer-protection enforcement, including possible fines of up to 6% of a company's worldwide annual turnover in major cross-border cases. Those powers aren't in effect either.

If the legislation passes, publishers will have to rethink at least some of their usual monetization systems in the EU. What survives the negotiations, particularly the rules for minors, will decide how big that change is.

After years of near radio silence, Fairgames has been canceled and its staff redistributed throughout Sony games.

#4399. Scientists discover a hidden warning sign of cannabis addiction

A new national study suggests that the way people consume cannabis may reveal important clues about their likelihood of using it heavily or developing an addiction. While smoking remains the most popular method among US adults who use cannabis, roughly one in seven consumes it in nearly every available form. Researchers found that this group had particularly high rates of daily use and cannabis use disorder.

Cannabis is consumed in several ways, including smoking, vaping, eating edibles, and dabbing, which involves heating concentrated cannabis products and inhaling the resulting vapor. Its use is widespread in the United States. Recent national survey figures indicate that approximately 43.8 million Americans ages 12 and older (more than 15 percent) had consumed cannabis within the previous 30 days.

Researchers at NYU Langone Health identified four distinct patterns of cannabis consumption. Nearly half of users, 48 percent, primarily smoked cannabis, while 21 percent combined smoking and vaping. Another 17 percent mainly consumed edibles. The remaining 14 percent belonged to what researchers called the "polymodal group," meaning they used cannabis in almost every available form.

Cannabis Addiction Rates Differ Sharply by Consumption Pattern

The findings, published online August 8 in the journal Addictive Behaviors, revealed major differences in how frequently these groups consumed cannabis. Approximately half of people in the polymodal group reported using it every day. Daily use was considerably less common among other participants, occurring in 28 percent of those who primarily smoked, 31 percent of those who smoked and vaped, and about 13 percent of those who mainly consumed edibles.

An even more striking difference emerged when researchers examined cannabis use disorder, the medical diagnosis associated with cannabis addiction. About 67 percent of polymodal users met the criteria for the disorder, compared with 47 percent of those who both smoked and vaped, 36 percent of those who mainly smoked, and just 15 percent of participants who primarily used edibles.

"Our findings suggest that using cannabis in multiple forms may be a red flag for heavier use and symptoms of addiction," said study lead author Omar El-Shahawy, MD, PhD, MPH, an assistant professor in the Department of Population Health at NYU Grossman School of Medicine. "Asking patients not only whether but how they use cannabis could help clinicians identify when a fuller assessment may be warranted."

To investigate these patterns, the research team examined responses from 17,732 adults who had used cannabis during the preceding month. The information came from the 2022-2023 National Survey on Drug Use and Health. Using statistical methods to identify similarities in participants' consumption habits, the researchers conducted the first national analysis of how different methods of cannabis use naturally group together.

Younger Adults More Likely to Use Multiple Forms of Cannabis

The researchers also discovered notable differences in the characteristics of people who preferred particular consumption methods. Young adults ages 18 to 25 accounted for nearly one-third of both the smoking and vaping group and the polymodal group. In contrast, only about one sixth of participants who primarily smoked cannabis belonged to that age range.

Edibles showed a different demographic pattern. Women made up more than half of those who mainly consumed edible cannabis products, and this method was particularly common among college graduates. However, the study did not investigate what motivated participants to choose specific consumption methods, leaving the reasons for these differences unresolved, according to Dr. El-Shahawy.

Another finding raised concerns about the potential effects of inhaling smoke. People who smoked cannabis were more likely to also smoke cigarettes than those who mainly vaped cannabis or consumed edibles. Because both tobacco and cannabis smoking involve combustion (burning), people who regularly smoke both substances may expose their lungs to additional harmful chemicals.

"The strong tie between smoking cannabis and smoking cigarettes is of concern because this subset of people are breathing in a wider range of chemicals via combustion, and their lungs are at risk," said senior author Joseph J. Palamar, PhD, MPH, a professor in the Department of Population Health at NYU Grossman School of Medicine.

Why Cannabis Prevention Messages May Need to Change

The findings suggest that health education should account for the different ways people consume cannabis rather than concentrating primarily on smoking. Different consumption patterns may call for different approaches to explaining potential risks, particularly among younger adults and people who regularly combine several methods.

"Public health messages about cannabis still focus mostly on smoking, but people now use the drug in many different ways," said Dr. El-Shahawy. "For younger adults, that means talking about the risks of vaping and combining multiple forms, while for people who prefer edibles, the message is to 'start low and go slow' because the effects take time to kick in."

The researchers hope to investigate the motivations behind these consumption patterns in future work. According to Dr. El-Shahawy, one question is whether people who favor edibles are more likely to use cannabis to manage problems such as pain or difficulty sleeping.

The team also emphasized several limitations. Because participants described their own cannabis habits, some may not have reported their consumption accurately or completely. The observational study also cannot determine whether using multiple forms of cannabis directly increases addiction risk. It establishes an association between consumption patterns and cannabis use disorder, rather than proving that one causes the other.

The research received funding from the National Institutes of Health through grant R01DA055675.

Additional NYU Langone researchers who contributed to the study included Mohsen Abbasi-Kangevari, MD, MPH; Michelle He; and Xiaoying Zheng, alongside Drs. El-Shahawy and Palamar. Neal Doran, PhD, of the University of California, San Diego, also served as a study co-investigator.

#4396. A little-known protein could be a major culprit in type 2 diabetes

Researchers have identified a protein that may play an important role in Type 2 diabetes by interfering with the body's ability to respond to insulin. The discovery could provide a promising new target for treatments designed to improve blood sugar control.

The protein, known as Miro1, was found at higher levels in the skeletal muscles of people with Type 2 diabetes. In preclinical experiments, scientists discovered that removing Miro1 restored the muscles' response to insulin. They also found that exercise lowered Miro1 levels in people with the disease, offering new insight into how physical activity improves insulin sensitivity.

The findings were published in Nature Communications and could help researchers better understand the biological processes behind insulin resistance, a central feature of Type 2 diabetes.

How a Hidden Muscle Protein Affects Insulin Resistance

Miro1 (Mitochondrial Rho GTPase1) is located on the outer membrane of mitochondria, the tiny structures inside cells responsible for producing energy. Researchers believe that excessive amounts of this protein may interfere with how muscles respond to insulin, making it more difficult for the body to regulate blood sugar effectively.

To investigate this connection, the research team studied Miro1 in laboratory cells, preclinical models, and people living with Type 2 diabetes. By examining the protein across these different settings, they were able to explore its effects on muscle function and determine whether the findings could be relevant to human disease.

The results showed that Miro1 buildup impaired the muscles' response to insulin. When researchers removed the protein in preclinical models, insulin responsiveness returned, providing evidence that Miro1 contributes directly to this process.

Exercise Reduces a Protein Linked to Type 2 Diabetes

The researchers also investigated whether exercise could influence Miro1 levels in people with diabetes. In a randomized controlled trial involving participants with obesity and Type 2 diabetes, they compared the effects of aerobic exercise with those of standard medical care.

People assigned to the exercise group experienced a decline in Miro1 levels in their muscles. These changes occurred alongside improvements in insulin sensitivity and the muscles' capacity to produce energy.

The findings suggest that reducing Miro1 may be one of the ways exercise helps the body respond more effectively to insulin. They also raise the possibility that treatments designed to target the protein could eventually provide additional benefits alongside physical activity.

"Insulin resistance in muscle is at the heart of Type 2 diabetes, and its molecular causes have remained frustratingly unclear. This study, the product of years of work, identifies Miro1 as a key part of the answer. By tracing Miro1 from cells to preclinical models to patients, we show that Miro1 accumulation impairs the muscle's response to insulin, that removing it causally restores that response in our models, and that exercise reverses its buildup in people. For the field, this is a new therapeutic target. For patients, it deepens our understanding of why exercise is so effective and opens a path toward treatments that could one day complement it," said Dr. John P. Kirwan, the study's senior author.

A Promising New Direction for Diabetes Treatment

Kirwan recently became executive director of the OU Health Harold Hamm Diabetes Center at the University of Oklahoma. He carried out the research while working at LSU's Pennington Biomedical Research Center and has since brought his internationally recognized translational research program to the University of Oklahoma.

He also serves as Vice Provost for Diabetes Programs at the university and holds the Chickasaw Nation Endowed Chair in Diabetes Research.

The study's first author, Elizabeth Heintz, is a doctoral candidate who worked in the Integrated Physiology and Molecular Medicine Laboratory at Pennington Biomedical. Christopher Axelrod, the study's co-corresponding author, has also moved to the Harold Hamm Diabetes Center, joining Kirwan in continuing this line of research.

Dr. Jennifer Rood, Interim Senior Vice Chancellor and Executive Director of Pennington Biomedical, emphasized the importance of connecting laboratory discoveries with research involving patients and broader populations.

"This research exemplifies the breadth of scientific discovery at Pennington Biomedical, where research spans all levels, from basic science that reveals the biological mechanisms underlying disease to clinical studies and population-based research that informs public health," said Dr. Jennifer Rood, Interim Senior Vice Chancellor and Executive Director of Pennington Biomedical. "Dr. Kirwan and his team's findings on Miro1 demonstrate the value of this integrated approach, connecting fundamental discoveries about muscle function with insights into insulin resistance and the benefits of exercise in people with Type 2 diabetes. This work is advancing our understanding of diabetes and helping lay the foundation for future approaches to prevention and treatment."

Could Targeting Miro1 Lead to New Diabetes Therapies?

Although the results are encouraging, scientists still need to establish whether directly targeting Miro1 can produce safe and effective treatments for people with Type 2 diabetes. The restoration of insulin responsiveness was demonstrated in preclinical models, while the human trial showed that exercise reduced Miro1 levels alongside improvements in insulin sensitivity.

Kirwan plans to continue investigating these findings at the Harold Hamm Diabetes Center. His research will combine laboratory experiments with studies involving people to uncover more of the biological mechanisms responsible for diabetes and explore new strategies for preventing and treating the condition.

"Type 2 diabetes is an affliction in Oklahoma and nationally," he said. "Ultimately, we are looking for cures, and we hope these recent findings could be part of the solution."

The study received funding from the National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases, the National Institute on Aging, the National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health, the National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute, and the National Institute of General Medical Sciences.

#4393. Arc Raiders' new map will be unlocked through a community event that starts today, and everyone has to donate

Breaking New Ground is the name of that event, and it’s one where everyone will need to contribute in order to rebuild some old tunnels and unlock the way to Stella Montis.

Even beyond the ultimate goal of unlocking the new map, donations will also reward you with Merits, which is a new event currency, though there’s a cap on how many you can earn.

Once enough materials have been collected, the next phase of the event, Staking Our Claim, will begin, which will bring a new progression track to the game, and make Stella Montis available for players to visit.

Developer Embark describes the new environment as unlike any that we have seen in the game so far. It’s a facility carved into the northern mountains, which means it’s going to have a near-pristine look; quite the contrast with the rest of the game’s environments.

Stella Montis also has its own Arc enemies, loot, schematics, and other gameplay items. You can look forward to coming across the Shredder, a close-quarter Arc unit exclusive to the new map for now.

Then there’s The Matriarch, a somehow even larger version of the Queen. Thankfully, it will only be available under a specific map condition, so you’re in no danger of running into her randomly. The update will also introduce a new legendary weapon, two new grenades, and three new mines.

Staking Our Claim will only run until December, which is when the next stage of the game’s roadmap will kick off. Then, the Cold Snap update will introduce the Flickering Flames event, the first snowfall Map Condition, and the Expedition Project voluntary wipe.

#4392. Eating less protein could slow aging, review of 350 studies finds

Protein is everywhere these days. From breakfast cereals and coffee to bottled water, manufacturers are adding extra protein to an expanding range of everyday products. But while consumers are being encouraged to eat more of it, a major scientific review suggests that cutting back on protein could offer surprising benefits for health and longevity.

After examining more than 350 scientific papers, researchers found evidence that reducing protein intake may help slow biological aging, improve metabolism, and, under certain conditions, extend lifespan. The potential benefits appear to involve several processes that influence how the body uses energy, responds to nutrients, protects cells from damage, and maintains healthy cellular function.

The findings, published in the Cell Press journal Cell Press Blue, raise an important question about the growing enthusiasm for high-protein diets. Could many people be consuming far more protein than their bodies actually need?

"It's absolutely crystal clear that there are benefits of protein to muscle growth and exercise response of active individuals," says Dudley Lamming, the paper's corresponding author, of the University of Wisconsin-Madison. "But because most people are relatively sedentary, many people are likely consuming more protein than they actually need, which probably has negative health consequences."

Why Eating Less Protein Could Promote Longevity

Scientists have long understood that reducing calorie intake can extend lifespan in numerous organisms. Research has also linked calorie restriction to a lower risk of diseases associated with aging, including cancer. However, consistently eating fewer calories is challenging, making it difficult for many people to maintain such a diet over time.

An alternative approach has attracted increasing scientific interest: reducing protein without necessarily eating less food.

Experiments involving flies and rodents have demonstrated that limiting protein intake can increase lifespan even when total calorie consumption remains unchanged. This suggests that the benefits of dietary restriction may depend not only on how much food is consumed, but also on which nutrients make up that food.

Human research has produced encouraging findings as well. Several recent clinical trials have shown that people who reduce their protein intake can lose weight, decrease body fat, and improve fasting blood sugar levels, even when they consume more calories overall. Fasting blood sugar measures glucose in the bloodstream after a period without eating and is an important indicator of metabolic health.

These findings do not establish that protein restriction extends human lifespan, but they suggest that changing protein intake can influence processes associated with aging and disease.

The Debate Over How Much Protein We Really Need

The picture becomes more complicated when exercise and muscle health enter the equation.

Other studies have demonstrated that higher protein intake can support weight loss and help older adults preserve muscle mass, particularly when combined with physical activity. Maintaining muscle becomes increasingly important with age because muscle loss can contribute to weakness, reduced mobility, and a greater risk of falls.

Research highlighting these benefits helped motivate US authorities to revise dietary recommendations this year, encouraging daily protein consumption of 1.2-1.6 grams per kilogram of body weight (0.5-0.7 grams per pound). That represents nearly twice the previous recommended amount.

With protein consumption reaching new highs in the United States and older adults increasingly being advised to eat more, Lamming and a colleague examined decades of research to better understand the relationship between protein intake and aging.

Their analysis brought together findings from more than 350 papers, identifying several biological mechanisms that repeatedly appeared across studies. Together, these mechanisms suggest that lowering protein consumption may improve metabolic function, alter the way cells detect nutrients, limit cellular damage, and help preserve the processes that keep cells functioning properly.

A Hormone That May Help Explain Slower Aging

One particularly intriguing finding involves fibroblast growth factor 21 (FGF21), a hormone that becomes more abundant when dietary protein is limited.

FGF21 helps the body adjust to changes in nutrient availability and influences how energy is used. Higher levels of this hormone can increase energy expenditure, support healthier blood sugar regulation, and reduce inflammation.

These effects are especially interesting because metabolism and chronic inflammation are closely connected to aging. Over time, disruptions in these processes can contribute to conditions such as obesity, diabetes, and other age-related diseases.

Studies in mice have shown that animals with elevated FGF21 levels live longer than mice with normal levels. The lifespan benefit was particularly strong in males, suggesting that biological sex may influence how the body responds to this hormone.

Researchers have also established that eating less protein increases FGF21 levels in humans. Whether this hormonal response produces the same longevity benefits seen in mice remains an important unanswered question.

How Certain Amino Acids Could Influence Aging

The amount of protein someone eats may not be the only factor that matters. The types of amino acids that make up that protein could also play an important role.

Amino acids are the building blocks the body uses to produce proteins, which are essential for maintaining muscles, repairing tissues, and carrying out countless cellular functions. Beyond these basic roles, certain amino acids also act as signals that influence metabolism and cellular growth.

The review identifies three amino acids that appear especially important: methionine, isoleucine, and valine.

Research suggests that excessive intake of these amino acids can stimulate biological pathways that encourage growth. Although growth-related processes are essential for normal development and tissue repair, excessive or prolonged activation of certain pathways may contribute to obesity, inflammation, and other conditions associated with aging.

Limiting specific amino acids could therefore produce some of the benefits observed in protein-restricted diets. This possibility has attracted attention because it suggests that the relationship between protein and longevity may be more complicated than simply eating more or less of a single nutrient.

"These studies show that the amount of protein sedentary people are eating today may have negative health consequences, at least at the population level," Lamming says.

Why Exercise Could Change the Effects of Protein

The researchers emphasize that protein requirements are not the same for everyone.

Pregnant women, for example, need additional protein to support fetal development, while some older adults require higher amounts to help maintain muscle and physical function. People who exercise regularly may also benefit from greater protein consumption because their muscles use those nutrients to recover, repair tissue, and adapt to training.

For many adults who spend most of their day sitting, however, adding protein to everyday foods may offer little additional benefit.

Lamming points out that athletes frequently consume large amounts of protein without developing the metabolic diseases sometimes associated with protein-rich diets. One possible explanation is that physical activity changes how the body handles those nutrients.

Regular exercise stimulates muscle growth and repair, potentially allowing the body to put additional protein to productive use while reducing some of the harmful metabolic effects associated with high protein intake.

This distinction may help explain why studies sometimes reach seemingly contradictory conclusions about protein. A diet that benefits someone who exercises intensely may not be ideal for someone with a largely sedentary lifestyle.

Rather than recommending the same amount of protein for everyone, the researchers argue that dietary advice should better reflect individual circumstances, especially physical activity levels and age.

"Recent recommendations have encouraged people to eat more protein, but they've also encouraged people to exercise more," Lamming says. "We probably need to personalize protein recommendations based not just on age, but also on how physically active people are."

The findings challenge the assumption that adding more protein automatically leads to better health. Although protein remains essential, the growing body of longevity research suggests that for some people, consuming less may offer benefits that have been overlooked in the rush toward protein-rich foods.

The work was supported by the National Institute on Aging, the Wisconsin Partnership Program, and the University of Wisconsin-Madison.

#4391. We Explored the Ford Vault, the New Home of Ford’s Heritage Fleet

From classics like the Model T to concept cars and race cars, the Vault is full of wonders.

Up until recently, Ford didn’t have an official collection of its many important historical vehicles. That all changed when Ford started curating its Heritage Fleet in 2024, and we got our first sneak peek at the collection in 2025. Now, however, Ford has moved the fleet into a new permanent home: the Ford Vault.

Situated in a nondescript building in Romulus, Michigan, the Ford Vault will house the Heritage Fleet, which includes everything from Model Ts and Mustang prototypes to race cars and one-off concepts. Currently, due to zoning laws, the building is only open to employees and offers limited opportunities for media, with the site formerly used as an Amazon warehouse.

However, Ford promises that it is working with the Romulus city government to get the building up to code so it can be turned into a public museum. The company didn’t provide a timeline for when the collection would open up to the public, but we got to take an early look at the fleet it has amassed.

See all results for used Ford for sale near 19047

Many of the cars were already part of the collection that we saw back in 2025, but Ford also brought in several new vehicles. We’re not going to cover any of the vehicles we wrote about back in 2025, so if you’re interested in what else Ford has in its Heritage Fleet, go check out that roundup below.

See More Cars from the Ford Heritage Fleet

Ford built more than 15 million Model Ts, but this one stands out for two reasons. For starters, this Model T was sold in the United Kingdom, meaning it has the steering wheel on the right. You’ll also notice that instead of the customary black paint job, this Model T wears a vibrant green hue. Henry Ford’s famous line of “any color, so long as it’s black” didn’t actually come into effect until 1914, once the groundbreaking assembly line was up and running. Before then, you could order the Model T in red, green, blue, and grey. Black paint dried faster, leading Ford to restrict the color palette once the assembly line was bustling for the sake of efficiency.

The Super Chief concept is the complete opposite of the bare-bones Model T. Designed as a vision for a luxury truck in an era when pickups were transitioning from workhorses to lifestyle vehicles, the concept took inspiration from the Super Chief locomotives of the 1950s for its domineering look. Under the hood, it used an innovative supercharged 6.8-liter V-10 called “Tri-Flex” because it could combust gasoline, E85, or hydrogen. Coach doors open to reveal a decadent cabin covered in brown leather, brushed aluminum, and American walnut wood. The glass roof sits over a structured grid of leather and wood, while the bed is lined with wood and strips of metal.

See all results for used Ford for sale near 19047

From the front, this may look like a normal Mustang GT350, but once you get to the rear, you’ll find that it has actually been converted into a pickup truck. This Mustang Ute project was built by apprentices in Ford’s metal shop at its Experimental Vehicles Building as a way to train them on the complexities of building concept cars. It uses the bed from a Ranger, and while it was never destined to be more than a training exercise, the Ute now has us daydreaming about a hi-po successor to the Falcon Ute sold in Australia until 2016.

The Model T isn’t the only foreign-market car in the collection. This is the adorable first-generation Ka, a tiny hatchback sold in Europe from 1996 to 2008. In fact, this was the final first-gen Ka to roll off the production line, and it has fewer than 10 miles on the odometer, making it probably the most pristine Ka in existence. The Ka was a big success for Ford, and it even spawned a convertible called the StreetKa, which we’d love to see added to the collection in the future.

Ford has called its upcoming Fathom electric truck a “Model T moment,” but this isn’t the first time the company has employed such language. The 2003 Model U concept was designed as a modern take on the Model T’s “people’s car” approach. It was a small pickup truck that could be transformed into an SUV via a retractable rear section. It also had a retractable canvas roof and exterior body panels made from a soy-based material. Under the hood lived a supercharged 2.3-liter four-cylinder hydrogen-combustion engine mated to an electrified automatic transmission. The Model U got a claimed 45 mpg and was loaded with features that weren’t yet common in 2003, from a head-up display to adaptive headlights and automatic emergency braking.

The Ford Bronco was killed off in 1996, but by 1999 there were already plans to bring the off-roader back. Designer Moray Callum led a team that proposed this next-generation Bronco, known under the codename U260. It was based on a Ranger platform, but never progressed much beyond this exterior-styling prototype. Ford would revisit the Bronco in 2004 with a concept that debuted at the Detroit auto show, which also lives in the Heritage Fleet, but we’d have to wait until 2021 to see the Bronco name return on a production car.

Love it or hate it, the SYNus is certainly one of the most unique-looking vehicles to ever wear the Blue Oval. While it looks like it should be pronounced like “sinus,” the name is actually meant to be said “sin-you-ehs,” combining “synthesis” and US, standing for “Urban Sanctuary.” The design looks like a bank vault on wheels, with thin windows, slab-sided bodywork, and even a wheel handle for the rear door. While it looks imposing in photos, the SYNus is actually quite small in person, only measuring 158 inches long. It was powered by a 134-hp 2.0-liter four-cylinder mated to a five-speed manual.

These days, Lincoln only sells SUVs, but back in the ’90s, the luxury division considered building a two-door roadster. The L2K began as a proposal for a Mercury sports car, before Ford brass changed their mind. Built on a heavily modified chassis from a 1993 Mazda Miata, the L2K packed a 250-hp 3.4-liter V-8 engine and a four-speed automatic. The L2K was a drivable concept, and it reportedly completed around 100 laps of Saugus Speedway in Santa Clarita, California. It then debuted at the Los Angeles auto show and toured the show circuit before management scrapped the project. While there were reports that the L2K was scrapped, the slinky Lincoln clearly survived.

This pointy concept from 1963 is actually based on a Shelby Cobra, eschewing the iconic curvaceous body for a wedge shape. Designed by Eugene Bordinat, Ford’s head of styling at the time, the Cougar II’s fastback fiberglass body looks sleek and modern, with a rich red paint job accented by chrome trim. The Cougar II also wore pop-up headlights, and improved aerodynamics meant it could allegedly hit 170 mph (10 more than a standard 260 V-8-powered Cobra). The Cougar II and a similar concept, the Bordinat Cobra, are on loan from the Detroit Historical Society, and the Ford Vault may include more vehicles on loan for rotating exhibits once it opens to the public.

Many of Ford’s concept cars feature experimental powertrains, and the Reflex is no exception. This futuristic-looking compact coupe was motivated by a diesel-electric hybrid engine with innovative-for-the-time lithium-ion batteries. Ford claims the Reflex could return 65 mpg, and with an electric motor on the rear axle providing all-wheel drive, 60 mph arrived in a claimed 7.0 seconds. Opening the rear-hinged butterfly doors reveals a cabin that looks inspired by athletic wear, with lightweight seats upholstered in mesh and rubber in the floor taken from Nike shoes. The Reflex also has a 2+1 layout, with a single “love seat” mounted behind the front passengers, along with an integrated child seat and a baby camera monitor mounted in the dash. Sadly, this mixture of sporty and practical never made it into production.

We’ll close with a trio of vehicles that won’t be in the Vault beyond the next few days, but are too good to not include. These are the three Ford GT40 race cars that, somewhat controversially, crossed the finish line together to take the top three spots at the 1966 24 Hours of Le Mans. The legendary finish saw the black No. 2 Shelby American car driven by Bruce McLaren take first place ahead of Ken Miles in the blue-and-red No. 2, who had been leading for much of the race’s final hours and had been asked to slow so that the three leading GT40s could finish together.

Caleb Miller began blogging about cars at 13 years old, and he realized his dream of writing for a car magazine after graduating from Carnegie Mellon University and joining the Car and Driver team. He loves quirky and obscure autos, aiming to one day own something bizarre like a Nissan S-Cargo, and is an avid motorsports fan.

Bandai Namco has announced that it is shutting down one of its studios, Reflector Entertainment. Perhaps one of the lesser-known studios under Bandai Namco’s wing, Reflector Entertainment has yet to show its potential.

The latest and only project by Reflector Entertainment is Unknown 9: Awakening, which rolled out in October 2024. It’s an action-adventure where you step into the shoes of Haroona, who is able to enter a mysterious dimension that overlaps our own, and she can channel numerous powers on her quest.

Tripwire Interactive has been hit with layoffs for a second time this year, but it has been confirmed that work continues on Killing Floor 3 and Maneater 2.

The game is just one of many parts of the IP’s narrative universe, as there are also stories told across podcasts, comics, novels, and web series.

Bandai Namco acquired Reflector Entertainment in 2020, and even though the studio is based in Canada, Reflector joined the family over at Bandai Namco Europe. At the time of the acquisition, the studio was already working on Unknown 9: Awakening. After Unknown 9: Awakening’s weak reception among fans and critics, Reflector Entertainment announced that 18% of its staff were being laid off, just one month after the game’s launch.

Unknown 9: Awakening sits at a Top Critic Average of 62 on OpenCritic, along with just 17% of critics recommending the game. Of course, that’s less than ideal, especially with the backing of Bandai Namco, who are known for delivering some of the biggest franchises, including Dark Souls, Code Vein, Dragon Ball video games, and so much more.

The reason given for the liquidation of Reflector Entertainment was that it came as part of a continuous review into The Group’s business portfolio, and “after comprehensively considering future business plans, necessary additional investment, and the possibility of profitability and business continuation, the Company has decided to discontinue Reflector’s business, dissolve and liquidate it.”

The statement clarifies that a concrete liquidation schedule “is undecided as of now. The Company will advance the necessary procedures according to local laws and regulations, and once said procedures are completed, the liquidation will be complete.”

The matter comes with huge losses for Bandai Namco, as they expect to “post an extraordinary loss of approximately 21 million euros (approx. 3.5 billion yen) on its consolidated financial statements for the third quarter (nine months) of the fiscal year ending March 31, 2027, and thereafter.” The final figure and timing remain under review, but the impact will be eye-watering, nevertheless.

After Unknown 9: Awakening’s weak reception among fans and critics, Reflector Entertainment announced that 18% of its staff were being laid off, just one month after the game’s launch.

It’s unknown how many employees are impacted by the closure of Reflector Entertainment, and at the time of writing, Reflector Entertainment has yet to comment on its liquidation.

Sadly, Reflector Entertainment joins a long list of studios to be shut down or hit with layoffs this year. As a result of the XBOX layoffs, for example, two separate agreements to sell off the creators behind Hellblade, Ninja Theory, fell through. As a result, the studio is facing a proposed closure.

Consultation with Arkane Lyon, the team behind Dishonored and the upcoming Marvel’s Blade game, remains underway and is expected to continue through the end of the year.

Despite Ghost of Yotei's resounding success, an eighth of the team has been laid off.

#4385. Cancer-fighting chewing gum slashes HPV levels by up to 93%

A specially engineered chewing gum could offer an unexpected new weapon against viruses and bacteria linked to head and neck cancer. In laboratory tests using samples from cancer patients, researchers found that extracts from the gum reduced levels of human papillomavirus, or HPV, by as much as 93%. An enhanced version also nearly eliminated two harmful bacterial species while leaving beneficial bacteria unharmed.

The findings, reported in Scientific Reports, suggest that this experimental approach could eventually help prevent certain infections and support existing cancer treatments. Researchers believe the plant-based technology could also provide a more affordable option for patients.

The research was led by Henry Daniell of the University of Pennsylvania's School of Dental Medicine. His team has been exploring ways to use specially engineered plants to produce proteins with potential medical benefits.

Why Scientists Are Targeting Cancer-Linked Microbes

Head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC) is a common form of cancer that develops in the tissues lining the mouth and throat. It begins in squamous cells, the thin, flat cells that cover many surfaces throughout the body. These cancers can be particularly difficult to treat once they have spread, and patients diagnosed at advanced stages often face poor outcomes.

According to Daniell, recently approved cancer medications have generally failed to produce major improvements in patients' quality of life or their chances of surviving five years after diagnosis. This highlights the continuing need for more effective treatments and new strategies that could help prevent the disease or reduce complications.

One promising area of research involves the microorganisms living in the mouth. Although many oral microbes are harmless or beneficial, certain viruses and bacteria have been associated with the development or progression of head and neck cancers.

The researchers focused on three of these microbes. The first was HPV, a common virus that can cause certain cancers when infections persist. The other two were Porphyromonas gingivalis (Pg) and Fusobacterium nucleatum (Fn), bacterial species associated with oral disease and poorer outcomes in some cancer patients.

"The global increase in oropharyngeal cancer is linked to HPV infection," says Daniell. "And Pg and Fn infections worsen survival rates of untreated recurrent or metastatic oral cancer, even after surgery and risk-adjusted adjuvant, or supplemental, therapies."

Oropharyngeal cancer affects the middle portion of the throat, including areas such as the tonsils and base of the tongue. Metastatic cancer refers to cancer that has spread beyond its original location, while adjuvant treatments are additional therapies given to improve the effectiveness of primary treatment.

A Chewing Gum Made From Beans Delivers Surprising Results

The new study builds on the team's earlier development of a chewing gum made from lablab beans (bean gum). This gum contains FRIL, a naturally occurring protein with antiviral properties.

To investigate its potential benefits, the scientists tested extracts from the gum against microbes found in oral samples collected from patients with head and neck cancer.

The results were striking. The bean gum extracts lowered HPV levels by 93% in saliva samples and by 80% in oral rinse samples. These findings suggest that proteins delivered through a chewing gum could potentially help reduce the presence of a virus associated with certain head and neck cancers.

The team then took the technology a step further by engineering the gum to contain protegrin, an antimicrobial peptide. Peptides are short chains of amino acids, the building blocks of proteins. Some antimicrobial peptides can attack and destroy harmful microorganisms, making them promising candidates for new infection treatments.

With this additional ingredient, the researchers found that a single dose of the engineered gum extract reduced the two targeted bacterial species, Pg and Fn, to almost undetectable levels.

Harmful Bacteria Nearly Disappear While Good Bacteria Survive

One of the most encouraging findings was the gum's ability to target harmful bacteria without disrupting the beneficial microorganisms that naturally inhabit the mouth.

The oral microbiome, the community of bacteria and other microscopic organisms living inside the mouth, plays an important role in maintaining oral health. Many of these microbes coexist harmlessly with the body and help maintain a balanced environment.

Some cancer treatments can disturb that balance. Radiation therapy, for example, can reduce populations of beneficial oral bacteria while encouraging the growth of potentially harmful yeast, including Candida albicans.

In contrast, the experimental gum extract sharply reduced the targeted bacteria without affecting the beneficial bacterial populations examined by the researchers. This selectivity could be especially valuable for patients whose oral health has already been affected by cancer or its treatment.

Importantly, the results came from laboratory testing of patient samples rather than clinical trials in which people chewed the gum. Further research will be needed to determine whether the same effects occur in the human mouth and whether reducing these microbes can meaningfully improve cancer outcomes.

Could Chewing Gum Become Part of Cancer Prevention and Treatment?

The researchers believe their findings justify moving the technology toward human clinical trials, particularly because head and neck cancers remain a serious global health challenge.

"Lip and oral cavity cancer was the seventh leading cancer type in cancer incidence and mortality rate worldwide in adolescents, young adults, and middle-aged adults in 2022," says Daniell. "Our findings support the value of advancing these therapies to clinical trials as adjuvants with current treatments or as prophylaxis to prevent infection and transmission."

Prophylaxis refers to measures taken to prevent disease or infection before it occurs. In this case, the researchers envision a future in which specially designed chewing gum might help limit exposure to harmful microbes or reduce their levels in people already receiving cancer treatment.

Such an approach could offer a relatively simple and potentially inexpensive way to deliver protective proteins directly into the mouth, where the targeted microorganisms are found.

For now, the technology remains experimental, and there is no evidence yet that chewing the gum prevents or treats cancer in humans. Nevertheless, the ability to substantially reduce HPV and nearly eliminate two cancer-associated bacterial species in laboratory tests offers a promising starting point for further investigation.

If future clinical trials confirm its safety and effectiveness, a familiar everyday product could become an unexpected addition to the medical toolkit against dangerous oral infections and cancers.

Henry Daniell is the W.D. Miller Professor in the Department of Basic & Translational Sciences at the School of Dental Medicine at the University of Pennsylvania.

Other authors are Geetanjali Wakade, Rahul Singh, and Smruti Nair of Penn Dental Medicine; Andrés M. Bur and Sufi M. Thomas of the University of Kansas Medical Center; Eri S. Srivatsan and Marilene B. Wang of the University of California at Los Angeles; and Saroj K. Basak of the Veterans Administration Greater Los Angeles Healthcare System.

#4382. Common osteoporosis drugs linked to 24% lower dementia risk in major study

A common class of drugs used to treat osteoporosis may have an unexpected benefit: lowering the risk of Alzheimer's disease and other forms of dementia. In a study involving more than 120,000 older adults, researchers at the University of Hong Kong (HKUMed) found that patients taking certain medications to strengthen their bones were significantly less likely to develop dementia.

The medications, known as nitrogen-containing bisphosphonates (NBPs), are widely prescribed to prevent bone loss and fractures. The findings suggest that these established treatments could potentially serve a second purpose by helping protect the aging brain. The research, conducted by scientists in the Department of Pharmacology and Pharmacy at HKUMed's LKS Faculty of Medicine, was published in Alzheimer's & Dementia.

More than 55 million people worldwide currently live with dementia, and that number is projected to climb to 139 million by 2050. The World Health Organization has identified dementia as a major global health priority. Although the first medications designed to slow the progression of Alzheimer's disease and related dementias (ADRD) have recently gained approval, their high costs, limited suitability for some patients, and questions about their effectiveness remain important challenges.

These obstacles have increased interest in finding affordable ways to prevent or delay dementia before symptoms develop. One promising approach is to identify existing medications that might offer benefits beyond the conditions they were originally designed to treat.

The Surprising Connection Between Bone Health and Dementia

Osteoporosis and dementia often affect the same older adults. Osteoporosis causes bones to become weaker and more vulnerable to fractures, while dementia progressively affects memory, thinking, and the ability to carry out everyday activities. The two conditions also share several risk factors, including older age, being female, and low levels of physical activity.

Previous research by the same HKUMed team established that osteoporosis and fractures are independent risk factors for dementia. The researchers also found that people already living with dementia face an increased likelihood of falling and breaking bones.

This relationship raises an intriguing possibility: medications that treat osteoporosis might also help reduce dementia risk.

Among the most commonly prescribed osteoporosis treatments are alendronate and zoledronate, both of which belong to the NBP drug class. These medications work by slowing the breakdown of bone tissue, helping maintain bone strength and reduce the likelihood of fractures.

Scientists have also begun uncovering evidence that some of the biological processes influenced by these drugs may be involved in the development of Alzheimer's disease and related dementias. This overlap has prompted researchers to investigate whether NBPs might provide benefits for the brain as well as the skeleton.

Study of 120,000 Patients Finds Up to 24% Lower Dementia Risk

To explore this possibility, the HKUMed researchers examined electronic medical records from across Hong Kong, analyzing data from more than 120,000 patients aged 60 and older. All participants had osteoporosis or fragility fractures, which are breaks that can occur after relatively minor injuries because the bones have become weakened.

The records covered the period from 2005 through 2020, allowing the team to investigate how different osteoporosis treatments were associated with dementia risk over time.

The results revealed a notable difference. Patients taking NBPs had a 16% lower risk of developing Alzheimer's disease and related dementias compared with patients who received no osteoporosis medication.

The association was even stronger when NBP users were compared with patients taking other types of osteoporosis drugs. In that comparison, dementia risk was 24% lower among those receiving NBPs.

Women and patients who had experienced hip fractures appeared to show particularly strong associations between NBP treatment and reduced dementia risk.

The researchers also estimated that treating 48 patients with NBPs over five years could potentially prevent one case of dementia. If future research confirms that the medications directly reduce dementia risk, the implications could be substantial, particularly for older adults who already need treatment for osteoporosis.

Because the findings come from an observational study, they do not establish that the drugs themselves prevent dementia. However, they provide evidence supporting further investigation into whether these medications could help delay or prevent cognitive decline.

Could Existing Osteoporosis Drugs Help Prevent Alzheimer's?

Professor Cheung Ching-lung, Associate Professor in the Department of Pharmacology and Pharmacy at HKUMed, believes the findings highlight the possibility that a familiar osteoporosis treatment could deliver two important health benefits.

"Our study provides evidence that NBPs may offer dual benefits in strengthening bones and reducing fracture risk, as well as potentially preventing ADRD. Their potential neuroprotective role provides an empirical basis and supports future research on the actual effectiveness of this medication in preventing or delaying cognitive decline associated with ADRD."

The potential advantage of this approach is that NBPs are already widely available and have an established history of use in treating osteoporosis. Rather than developing an entirely new medication from scratch, researchers could investigate whether these existing treatments offer additional protection for people at elevated risk of dementia.

The findings are particularly relevant as populations around the world grow older and the number of people affected by dementia continues to rise.

"These findings are significant as they demonstrate a potential approach for reducing dementia risk in a vulnerable population using safe and widely available NBPs. In our rapidly aging society, these findings suggest that while waiting for the novel therapies, existing medications can also provide additional protection for high-risk populations," said Professor Cheung.

Further studies will be needed to determine whether NBPs can directly prevent or delay Alzheimer's disease and related dementias. Nevertheless, the results suggest that medications already prescribed to protect aging bones may also have an important role to play in protecting brain health.

The research was led by Professor Cheung Ching-lung of the Department of Pharmacology and Pharmacy at HKUMed. Dr Sing Chor-wing, from the same department, served as the study's first author.

Additional researchers included Professor Chan Koon-ho, Dr Patrick Chiu Ka-chun, and Professor Kathryn Tan Choon-beng, all from the Department of Medicine in the School of Clinical Medicine at HKUMed.

Materials provided by The University of Hong Kong. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#4381. Battlefield 6 gets a new map today alongside major changes to controller aim assist, and even more weapon dispersion tweaks

Right on schedule, the latest Battlefield 6 patch has arrived to kick off the next stage of Season 1.

Battlefield 6’s first season has entered its second phase. The game received a major update earlier today, version 1.1.2.0, which delivers a host of changes to the game, many of which have been expected.

The update, of course, also adds new content to the game in the form of the map Eastwood, as well as new hardware and fresh features for the multiplayer sandbox.

We’ve known about the new content side of today’s patch for quite some time. The update kicks off the California Resistance stage of Season 1, which is the second of three. The new Eastwood map takes place in California, and it’s a map cut from the larger Battlefield Redsec battle royale map of Fort Lyndon.

There’s a new limited-time mode called Sabotage - a tactical, 8v8 mode where two teams attempt to destroy as many bomb sites as possible. The other big new feature that arrives today is Battle Pickups.

These are powerful weapons which can be found in specific game modes (and in Portal), scattered around the map for players to pick up and use. They have limited ammo that cannot be replenished, and deliver incredible firepower.

Redsec players have a new Gauntlet mission to look forward to that joins the existing modes. It’s called Rodeo and it involves a lot of vehicular action. Finally, everyone gets to unlock two new weapons: the the DB-12 shotgun, and the M327 Trait revolver sidearm. There’s also a new angled grip attachment.

The fixes and tweaks side of the patch is arguably the more interesting. Controller aim assist has received a big overhaul that essentially resets everything to open beta settings. The goal is to make infantry targeting more consistent.

Controller players actually get the bulk of the changes in this update, which also improves input latency and stick response. Several issues that reset aim assist values, or make it behave erratically, have been addressed.

The conversation around weapon bloom/spread doesn’t look like it’s ever going to end, because Battlefield Studios is yet again tuning gunplay to fix unintended dispersion behaviour, and decrease its intensity across the board.

Certain Challenges have had their description rewritten so their requirements can be better understood. Beyond that, you can expect several deployables to behave much more consistently, including several bug fixes there, too.

Head to the official blog for the full rundown of patch 1.1.2.0.

#4377. Battlefield 6 is getting a free trial next week with... a questionable selection of maps, but at least the modes are good

Presumably as a way of marching ever forward towards its (alleged) 100 million player goal for Battlefield 6, EA has announced that the multiplayer shooter will be getting its first free trial later this month.

This is, of course, specifically for players to sample the core, paid component of the game, as the recently launched Redsec remains free-to-play. Redsec, however, offers modes like battle royale and Gauntlet, which aren’t quite the traditional Battlefield experience.

The Battlefield 6 trial arrives next Tuesday, November 25. It will run for one week, ending the following Tuesday, December 2. The trial will be available on all platforms, but won’t include all content from the full game.

Instead, players will have access to three of the game’s maps and five of its modes. Siege of Cairo will be there alongside Season 1’s two new maps: Eastwood, and Blackwell Fields. It’s not the strongest line-up of maps, considering Eastwood is already cut from the larger Fort Lyndon battle royale map that Redsec players should be quite familiar with, but it’s something.

As for modes, you can pick from Conquest, Breakthrough, Sabotage, and Team Deathmatch. Battlefield Studios didn’t say what the fifth mode is going to be, but a dedicated blog post with more information is set to arrive next week.

Beyond the trial's content itself, the timing is certainly great. Battlefield 6 just received one of its biggest patches, kicking off the second phase of its first season. So far this season, we’ve seen two new maps, several new weapons - but more importantly, solutions to problems the game’s had since launch, as well as fixes to longstanding bugs.

The miserable XP progression Battlefield 6 launched with is far more tolerable. Challenges and Assignments are much easier to understand and actually finish. The often maligned weapon dispersion has been toned down. Some of the wildest vehicle bugs have been fixed. And Portal has a host of experiences that go beyond just bot farms.

In essence, Battlefield 6 feels like its reached its 1.0 status, which makes this a great entry point for new players, even if the trial could've used more of the game's better maps.

#4376. Ancient climate records reveal how East Asian monsoon shifted abruptly into cold and drought

How does climate change affect the East Asian monsoon? Researchers from Utrecht University's Faculty of Geosciences, together with colleagues at research institutes in China and Belgium, are investigating this question by looking back 250,000 years. They found that, over long timescales, the monsoon system tracks changes in incoming solar radiation caused by variations in Earth's orbit and tilt. But when radiation falls below a certain threshold, abrupt periods of extreme cold and drought occur, particularly when atmospheric CO₂ concentrations are low. The study was published in Communications Earth & Environment.

#4374. Caltech robot makes history by building a structure in space

For the first time, a robot has successfully assembled part of a structure in space without astronauts, demonstrating a technology that could dramatically change how large spacecraft and scientific instruments are built.

The robotic system was developed by researchers at the California Institute of Technology (Caltech) with funding from the Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency (DARPA). It is part of DARPA's Novel Orbital and Moon Manufacturing, Materials, and Mass-efficient Design (NOM4D) program, an initiative exploring ways to manufacture and assemble enormous structures directly in space.

Rather than relying on astronauts to connect individual pieces, the robot uses an automated arm to retrieve structural tubes and connecting joints from nearby storage dispensers. It then joins the components into repeating sections, called bays, that form a larger supporting framework known as a truss.

"This is the first time that a structure has been autonomously constructed in space," says Sergio Pellegrino, the Joyce and Krent Kresa Professor of Aerospace and Civil Engineering, the Lynn Booth and Kent Kresa Department of Aerospace Leadership Chair, the executive officer for aerospace, and a senior research scientist at JPL, which Caltech manages for NASA.

A Historic Step Toward Building Giant Structures in Space

Pellegrino leads Caltech's Autonomous In-Space Tensioned Reflector Assembly (ASTRA) demonstration. The robotic system has spent six months in orbit attempting to construct a reflector antenna measuring 1.4 meters across. Its design combines composite fiber tubes, aluminum connectors, and a lightweight reflective surface made from Kapton, a durable polymer film commonly used in spacecraft.

DARPA compares the assembly process to building with sophisticated versions of K'Nex or Tinkertoy construction toys. However, making a robot perform those same tasks reliably in the harsh environment of space presents a far greater engineering challenge.

The team encountered technical difficulties and scheduling constraints that prevented it from finishing the entire antenna. Nevertheless, the robot successfully assembled an initial section, providing evidence that this construction method can work in orbit. Researchers believe the same basic approach could eventually support much larger frameworks carrying enormous reflective surfaces.

The orbital experiment represents the third stage of DARPA's research program. During the first two stages, Caltech researchers developed the construction concept, worked out the engineering design, and verified its operation in laboratory experiments on Earth. The team then had less than 12 months to manufacture, test, and deliver the space hardware to Momentus Inc., the company hosting the payload.

"Developing a payload of this complexity on such a short timeline was an enormous undertaking for our small team," says Pellegrino, who is also co-director of the Space Solar Power Project, which aims to harvest solar power in space and wirelessly transmit it to Earth's surface. "As we wrap up the mission, we are finally able to start thinking about the new avenues of research opened by this demonstration."

Why Scientists Want to Build Enormous Structures in Orbit

The ability to assemble large structures directly in space could transform astronomy, communications, and space based energy systems.

For example, future telescopes could use enormous reflective surfaces to collect more light and observe extremely distant objects. Similar structures could also support powerful radio antennas, allowing scientists and engineers to build communications systems much larger than those that can currently be launched.

One of the greatest obstacles is the limited room available inside a rocket's fairing, the protective enclosure that surrounds its payload during launch. No matter how ambitious a spacecraft design might be, its components must somehow fit inside that confined space.

Traditionally, engineers have addressed this problem in two ways. They either fold large structures into compact packages that can unfold after reaching orbit, or they launch separate components and have astronauts assemble them in space. Both approaches impose practical limits on the size and complexity of the finished structure.

Robotic construction offers a third possibility. Instead of fitting an enormous telescope or antenna inside a rocket, engineers could transport its materials into orbit and assemble the complete system there.

DARPA's Plan for Kilometer-Scale Space Structures

DARPA established NOM4D in 2022 to investigate technologies that could eventually "ferry raw materials from Earth for in-orbit manufacturing," according to the program's website.

Caltech's ASTRA experiment is one of only two projects selected to advance to the program's third phase, which involves demonstrating construction technologies in orbit.

The other project, led by the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, will use a module attached to the International Space Station to investigate a technique for hardening carbon tubes in space. This could provide another way to manufacture structural components without having to complete every step on Earth.

"NOM4D's objective is to enable efficient, scalable construction of very large structures in space," said Andrew Detor, DARPA program manager for NOM4D, in a written statement. "By 'very large,' I mean hundreds of meters or kilometers in scale. Nothing approaching that scale can be achieved today."

Such structures could eventually be several football fields long or even extend for kilometers, far beyond the dimensions of conventional spacecraft.

How Caltech's Construction Robot Reached Space

ASTRA began its journey on March 30, 2026, when a SpaceX Transporter-16 mission launched from Vandenberg Space Force Base in California early that morning.

The robot traveled aboard Momentus Inc.'s Vigoride 7 orbital vehicle, which carried 10 separate payloads into low Earth orbit. ASTRA occupied approximately one cubic meter of space, a compact package containing both the assembly machinery and the materials required for construction.

Inside were two previously assembled truss bays, reinforced with diagonal tubes and connecting joints. The payload also included a robotic arm and motorized dispensers loaded with the parts needed to construct the remaining sections.

The successful launch was an emotional moment for the small engineering team watching from Earth. Jaden Suh, a former Caltech postdoctoral scholar who is now an assistant professor at the University of Texas at Austin, was moved to tears as the spacecraft carrying his team's work headed into orbit.

"As a child, I was super curious about and interested in space structures. Just like many other engineers working in this field, sending your stuff to space is what I've been dreaming of my entire life," Suh says. "I was extremely lucky to have the opportunity to work on this project, beginning from scratch. A lot of my original ideas are included in this system, and it was just incredible seeing it reach space."

Building a Structure Hundreds of Miles Above Earth

After ASTRA reached orbit, researchers began operating the system by transmitting instructions to its onboard computer through the Vigoride spacecraft.

The initial steps involved releasing the mechanisms that had secured the components during launch. The robot then extended the two previously assembled truss bays out of the machine and proceeded to construct a third bay using the onboard assembly system.

Three team members managed the construction commands from Earth: Charles Sommer, a former Caltech systems engineer; Alan Truong, a Caltech research engineer; and graduate student Tara Venkatadri (MS '24).

Although the robot carried out the assembly operations automatically, the researchers monitored its progress using photographs transmitted from orbit. When something went wrong, they examined the images, adjusted their instructions, and attempted the operation again.

These setbacks were an important part of learning whether the technology could function outside a controlled laboratory.

"That's basically the reason you do proof-of-concept testing. There are a lot of differences in the space environment compared to down on Earth," Suh explains. "There are always lots of little surprises."

To diagnose problems in orbit, the engineers relied on a second ASTRA system kept at Pellegrino's laboratory at Caltech. This backup unit, known as a flight spare, allowed researchers to recreate difficulties encountered by the spaceborne robot and experiment with possible solutions.

"Every time we confirm there is an issue in space, we come to the laboratory and try to mimic the problem on the ground," Sommer says.

Communication restrictions made troubleshooting especially challenging. The team could contact ASTRA only during approximately seven or eight brief periods each day, with each opportunity lasting about 15 minutes.

That meant engineers had to make the most of their limited communication windows. They used the laboratory twin to investigate problems, evaluate different solutions, and determine which adjustments were most likely to work. Once a solution was ready, they sent the revised instructions to the robot in orbit.

This process helped the team work through numerous unexpected difficulties while gathering valuable information about what future autonomous construction systems will need to operate more reliably.

ASTRA's intended construction process involves repeating a carefully coordinated series of movements.

First, the robotic arm retrieves structural components from their storage dispensers. It positions the tubes and joints on an assembly plate and connects them to create a new truss bay.

Once the framework is assembled, the robot is designed to attach a thin reflective film containing many tiny openings. This material forms two reflective cable nets that are held under tension against one another by springs, helping the resulting surface maintain its intended shape.

The special film was jointly invented by researchers at Caltech and the University of Pennsylvania, where the collaborating team was led by Professor Igor Bargatin.

Unlike the knitted metallic mesh typically used in reflectors designed to fold and unfold, the perforated film requires less tension to maintain its shape. That allows engineers to reduce the amount of supporting structure needed, potentially making the entire assembly substantially lighter.

Lower weight is especially valuable in space engineering because every additional kilogram increases the demands placed on a launch vehicle.

When a bay is finished and its reflective components have been prepared, the robotic system pushes the completed section outward into space. It then begins assembling the next bay.

The full ASTRA antenna design calls for 11 connected bays, each attached to the reflective nets and extended outward from the assembly system.

A Small Demonstration With Enormous Implications

Despite successfully demonstrating the construction technique, the researchers do not expect ASTRA to finish assembling all 11 bays before the mission concludes in December.

The experiment has revealed several ways the robotic hardware and assembly procedure could be simplified and improved. Even without a completed antenna, the team believes it has collected enough evidence to establish that the approach is technically feasible.

The implications extend well beyond the relatively small antenna used in this demonstration.

Future robotic construction systems could help scientists build gigantic space telescopes that collect more light, radio antennas capable of supporting advanced communications, and enormous solar arrays designed to capture sunlight in orbit.

Such solar power systems could potentially transmit collected energy wirelessly to receivers on Earth, an idea being explored through Caltech's Space Solar Power Project.

More broadly, the successful test suggests that the size of future space infrastructure may not always have to be dictated by the dimensions of the rockets used to launch its components.

"Once you get to the size limit where structures cannot be prebuilt on the ground and unfolded, you have to think about how to build them in space," Pellegrino says. "So, this work could be useful not only for astronomy and astrophysics but also for communications and other areas, such as building very large solar arrays for space solar power."

As a band, they’re incredibly flexible and talented, with a good part of that grit coming from Iwai’s incredible bass play. The future of the band is currently uncertain, especially with how sudden Iwai’s loss truly was.

Eikichi Iwai passed at age 57, a titan of his craft and an incredible musician across his pursuits, charming millions who played Final Fantasy 14 and all who followed his long history with the band Chirinuruwowaka, of which he was a founding member. Never one to slow down or stop making music, with his recent showing at the latest Japanese FF14 Fan Fest being cited as one of THE PRIMALS best ever showings.

After suffering a loss like Iwai’s, it’s important to remember just how lucky we are to enjoy such incredibly skilled artists in their primes. Final Fantasy 14 has its issues, but music has never been one of them, carrying many crucial emotional scenes with next-level tracks again and again.

Close in the Distance, A Long Fall, and Rise, all written by Masayoshi Soken, show a mastery of tone and emotion across an incredible range, perfectly putting players in the mindset of the current moment. THE PRIMALS’ own coverage of tracks like Footfalls and Dawntrail gives each song life, fueled by THE PRIMALS’ incredible energy.

I genuinely believe you could find someone who cites almost every song in Final Fantasy 14 as one of their favorites, and that’s amazing. The incredible display of artistry throughout the title is a large reason why it has lasted as long as it has with the massive fanbase it has cultivated.

With live service games and MMOs like Final Fantasy 14, it can be all too easy and lucrative to fall into the trappings of consumerism, focusing on the product rather than the art. FF really doesn’t have that issue. FF14 has always felt like a title guided by the artists who create it, and after the loss of such a powerful artist, it’s up to the rest of us to keep on that path. Rest in peace, Eikichi Iwai.

#4372. Battlefield 6 streamlines some of the most annoying Challenges yet again, takes out a few of them entirely

The easier and more accessible Battlefield Studios makes those Battlefield 6 Challenges, the better.

The work to continue streamlining Challenges in Battlefield 6 is clearly not done. Having just released a new patch - which already included several updates to Challenges and Assignments - Battlefield Studios has gone in and made even more changes.

This latest round includes far fewer tweaks, but quite surprisingly, it also removes a few of the more annoying ones from the game.

The updated list, which Battlefield shared on Twitter, includes changes to the dreaded Recon 2 headshots beyond 150m Challenge. Now, any headshot beyond 75m will count. Recon Expert 3 is another headshot-themed one that’s been updated, and now requires getting headshot kills beyond 125m, rather than the practically impossible beyond 200m that it required previously.

The Rapid Fire 2 Challenge, which required getting kills beyond 50m with Assault Rifles, has been changed so it now tracks anything beyond 40m. The painful ‘Inflict damage under 15m while hip-firing with Assault Rifles’ has been entirely replaced with one that requires - the far more sensible - inflicting damage while in ADS with Assault Rifles.

A couple of Challenges, such as the one that required suppressing enemies with LMGs, and another that wanted you to deal damage to laser-designated vehicles using lock-on weapons, have both been removed.

The journey to make Challenges and Assignments easier to complete has been a long one. Progression has been one of the key areas of criticism Battlefield 6 received at launch. The issue encompassed more than just slow player and weapon XP earn rates, it also prevented players from accessing new Training Paths for the various classes, and several of the game's weapons.

Battlefield Studios attacked the problem from multiple angles, initially boosting the XP players and their weapons would earn, before later reducing the requirements of the Challenges themselves. The developer continued to streamline those requirements over multiple patches, including majorly overhauling the system earlier this month.

It seems the studio is more confident than ever in the game, as it recently announced that Battlefield 6 will be getting its first free trial next week, offering players who do not own the full game access to iconic modes like Conquest, and Breakthrough - though on an unusual selection of maps.
