#4369. 10 Most Creative Traversal Abilities in Metroidvanias

Ronald is a video game journalist with more than 10 years of experience in the industry, working on several of the most important Spanish websites.

Movement abilities in Metroidvanias are a fundamental part of their appeal, determining both the pace of exploration and our ability to interact with the surrounding world.

The genre is built on understanding spaces, their composition, and how to traverse them, making movement a crucial variable regardless of the game's perspective, mechanics, or philosophy.

As a result, the possibilities a game enables for movement along the Cartesian plane largely determine how satisfying, tense, or rewarding a campaign will be, depending on its intended purpose.

Therefore, in order to pay homage to those video games that make the best possible use of the philosophy of moving from one place to another, here are the ten most creative traversal abilities in Metroidvanias.

One of the main problems games in this genre face when creating spectacular movement abilities lies in their limitations, as they have to be balanced so that they aren't too powerful.

For this reason, Silk Soar from Hollow Knight: Silksong is a masterpiece of design. Among all the powers in Metroidvanias that let you fly upwards, it's part of the few that properly contextualize the limits of its capabilities.

Not only do you acquire it in the game's last third, unexpectedly opening paths out of nowhere, but its use is also tied to your needle, requiring the presence of a ceiling to be used, so you can't just break the map's traversal in its entirety.

In terms of creativity, it's on the spectrum's simpler side, yet it solves a major verticality imbalance by granting you a great deal of ease in exploration without making you overpowered, which is a tremendous feat.

Going in the opposite direction from the previous entry, Pipistrello and the Cursed Yoyo is a constant display of reinterpreting Metroidvanias' most common forms of movement, with Walk the Dog being the crown jewel.

The game plays with yo-yo tricks to establish its mechanics, adapting them with thematic coherence to make you feel that, more than just having powers within a video game, you're learning new maneuvers to show off.

In this particular instance, it's as simple as being able to move orthogonally across the map at a greater speed, but this is maximized thanks to the bounce pads distributed throughout all areas that change your direction and make the ability the key to numerous puzzles.

Pipistrello and the Cursed Yoyo is brimming with ideas magnificently adapted to its setting, making it by far one of the most inventive Metroidvanias to come out this decade.

Well Dweller breaks one of the genre's cardinal rules by not including a double jump at any point in its story, though it compensates with a Slingshot mechanic that is simply mesmerizing.

The title allows you to throw your weapon and embed it in any surface to use it as a springboard and jump higher than usual, encouraging inquisitive and creative exploration in a truly compelling way.

Most of the game's movement is based on the biomes you find yourself in, whether in the form of bubbles, air currents, or elevators, and it works precisely because this direct yet versatile ability adapts to any situation.

Of course, it leaves you without any means of defense, but, like Kratos's Leviathan Axe, Well Dweller's matchstick flies back to you when you need it, which also leads to spectacular and almost cinematic moments when transitioning from platforming to combat.

If you're looking for games that subvert your expectations, try these eight Metroidvanias that totally reinvent themselves halfway through.

In terms of inventiveness, Animal Well is a couple of notches above the rest of the genre, with all its progression tools being as unique as they're rewarding.

Since the title is more puzzle-based than platforming-focused, most of its abilities are proportional to said distribution, but the Disc is a versatile component that you can use both to solve environmental puzzles and to traverse in seemingly impossible ways.

Throwing the frisbee and timing its trajectory to hop on and soar through the air never gets old, both because of how mechanically satisfying it is and because of all the paths mastering this skill opens up.

Animal Well is a sandbox where most of its castles are built through iteration and experimentation, but fortunately, you have the Disc on your side to make the journey faster, smoother, and more enjoyable.

Despite my reservations about Constance due to its short length and limited side content, its movement mechanics are some of the smoothest I've ever seen in the genre, with Paint Dive being the standout.

It functions as both a dash and a dematerialization of the character, allowing her to blend into the environment and pass through obstacles and hazards as a graceful mass of purple paint that seamlessly integrates with the surroundings.

In its abstract form, it's simply a directional boost, yet its execution is elevated by the environments, which force you to use the ability in increasingly diverse ways, ensuring it's more than just a regular push.

Given that platforming is Constance's forte, Paint Dive plays a prominent role throughout the entire campaign, making it a proportionally more important element of the game than many of the other abilities on this list.

From classic Resident Evil to Dark Souls, these are eight Non-Metroidvanias that heavily influenced the genre.

Returning to what I mentioned about Silk Soar and the problems of having very powerful abilities, the Crystal Arrows in Aeterna Noctis take the conversation to another level by granting you the power to teleport to wherever you aim them.

Certainly, they're used in many of the most excruciatingly difficult platforming sections the genre has ever seen, but also in one of the deepest movement systems.

Being able to chain together consecutive teleportations while fighting and traversing Aeterna's world quickly becomes a delight, especially once you get used to them and feel you've mastered their immeasurable offensive and defensive potential.

While Aeterna Noctis' structure doesn't fully capitalize on the Crystal Arrows, they remain magnificent and satisfying, surprisingly without ever breaking the game's sequence.

Castlevania: Symphony of the Night dares to take its most unusual ability and only make it necessary for a limited number of sections, yet the Mist Form remains an unforgettable memory for anyone who plays the game.

Becoming an incorporeal entity to pass through bars is the kind of power fantasy that only a character like Alucard can materialize, with the added significance of having achieved something so astonishing thirty years ago.

Although there aren't many mandatory instances where you must use it, the ability is a major surprise when you unlock it, primarily when it becomes an incredibly powerful toxic weapon that allows you to both move freely and eliminate all enemies in your path.

Years have passed, and I don't think I've ever been so impacted by unlocking a new ability, which only speaks to Castlevania: Symphony of the Night's timeless greatness.

Of all the innovations that Ori and the Blind Forest brought to the genre during the formative years when its heirs were still establishing themselves, Bash is undoubtedly the most prominent.

The ability to bounce off both enemies and projectiles to move omnidirectionally and reach new heights and locations is absurdly incredible from the very first minute to the last.

The mechanic was significantly improved in the sequel, yet its stellar and unprecedented appearance in the franchise's first title is a core memory of the genre, particularly due to its use in combat to stylize every fight sequence.

I must admit Ori and the Blind Forest isn't among my favorite Metroidvanias, though that doesn't stop me from acknowledging that, in terms of uniqueness, there's no other ability that truly compares to Bash.

If you're already tired of 2D side-scrolling games, I recommend you read about these ten best first-person Metroidvanias, ranked.

By 1994 standards, the existence of a video game of Super Metroid's caliber seems absolutely insane, as years have passed and the game remains so fresh and enjoyable that it's astonishing how ahead of its time it was.

People usually praise the Shinespark or the Morph Ball, which are masterful abilities by any measure, but I have to admit that what truly amazed me was the Grapple Beam and how wonderfully it utilizes Zebes' layout.

You spend much of the journey wondering what those strange cross-shaped blocks are for, and when you discover that they allow you to aim a beam that lets you swing freely, spin, and propel yourself at top speed, you can't help but be blown away.

Whether you played it back then or today, Super Metroid surprises you with its mastery at every turn, and there are so many ways I could have included it on this list that all I can do is stand up and applaud.

I'm going to lean towards modernity to define the top spot on this list and praise the work of MIO: Memories in Orbit, a contemporary masterpiece of the genre whose scale is truly breathtaking.

There are many reasons to say this, but unlocking the Striders, tendrils into legs and arms that can grab any surface to walk on walls, was the moment in its campaign when I realized I wasn't just playing a good Metroidvania.

Even though their use is limited by a stamina bar, thinking about the titanic effort it must have taken to craft each room of its vast map based on the eventual access to this omnipotent movement tool makes me dizzy.

Not only does it have fluid and pristine animation with perfect sound design, but it also blends seamlessly with exploration and platforming mechanics to make everything related to movement a true gift for players.

I've had many surprising moments with movement mechanics in the genre, yet the Striders in MIO: Memories in Orbit are unique while also being functional, powerful, and visually appealing, which is an elevated balance that's extremely difficult to achieve.

From the best bosses to essential lore explanations, these are eight Metroidvanias that hide their best content behind the most unexpected paths.

#4368. Arc Raiders patch nerfs the Deadline mine, ends the menace of the Venator

The first post-Stella Montis patch for Arc Raiders has arrived, and it predictably touches much of what people brought to the latest map.

Arc Raiders has received a new update today that’s almost entirely dedicated to balance and economy tweaks. Patch 1.3.0 arrived earlier across all platforms, coming in at just under 1GB. This is an especially interesting patch because many of the changes it makes can be seen as a response to player behaviour on Stella Montis, the game’s latest map, which just joined the roster last week.

Stella Montis is available for players who’ve put in a decent number of rounds, and its close-quarters, enclosed environments have essentially turned it into the new “PvP map”, where constant action can be found.

That, of course, also means that the map has exposed a few balance issues with some of the game’s weapons and tools. Case in point: the Venator, a pistol that saw a lot of use recently. The weapon is especially powerful when fully-upgraded, something Arc Raiders developer Embark said pushed it beyond what had been originally intended.

In today’s update, the Venator's fire rate is the thing getting hit the hardest, with each upgrade now offering slower gains to the weapon's rate-of-fire compared to the way things were. The weapon’s weight is also being increased to five from two.

Another powerful item players have been getting a lot of mileage out of recently has been the Deadline mine. Unlike the Venator, the Deadline is mainly a threat to Arc enemies, and it’s proven incredibly powerful against the largest and most fearsome, such as the Bastion, and Leaper. In fact, the mine was considered essential when taking down a Queen.

The patch vastly increases its purchase price, and makes it more difficult to craft by upping the amount each of its components requires. Perhaps the most effective nerf, however, is the reduction to the Deadline’s stock at traders from three to just one, which means you’re going to be seeing a lot less of it topside.

Beyond those specific changes, Embark has also tweaked explosive damage across the board. According to the developer, explosive damage was being applied to multiple parts at once, which trivialised some encounters.

This change mainly affects larger Arc units, such as the Bastion, allowing them to withstand more explosive damage before bits start coming off of them. The Hullcracker, one of the best explosive damage weapons, has also caught a nerf as part of that.

#4366. Common supplement could help fight psoriasis, scientists discover

A widely available nutritional supplement derived from vitamin B5 may offer a promising new approach to treating psoriasis, according to research from China. Scientists found that pantethine can calm immune cells involved in autoimmune inflammation, preventing psoriasis from developing in mice and improving symptoms in a small human clinical trial.

The findings, published October 27 in the Journal of Experimental Medicine (JEM), reveal an unexpected connection between cholesterol production and the immune system. By interfering with this process, pantethine may help reduce the excessive immune activity responsible for psoriasis and potentially other autoimmune diseases.

How Overactive Immune Cells Contribute to Psoriasis

At the center of the discovery are dendritic cells, specialized immune cells that help organize the body's defenses. These cells act as coordinators, identifying potential threats and directing other immune cells to respond.

Dendritic cells perform this role by capturing foreign substances called antigens and presenting them to T cells, which are immune cells that recognize specific threats. They also release chemical signals that recruit additional immune cells and trigger inflammation.

Although these activities are essential for fighting infections, problems can arise when dendritic cells become excessively active. Instead of helping protect the body, they can contribute to persistent inflammation and autoimmune diseases such as psoriasis.

"Emerging evidence highlights that metabolic pathways and their associated metabolites play vital roles in regulating immune cell function and autoimmune progression," says Wei-Na Zhang, a researcher at the State Key Laboratory of Biomedical Analysis in Beijing. "But therapeutic strategies targeting metabolism in inflammatory diseases remain underexplored."

Zhang led the research alongside Qing Xia, Ai-Ling Li, and Tao Zhou, also from the State Key Laboratory of Biomedical Analysis, and Cheng-Xin Li from The First Medical Center of Chinese PLA General Hospital in Beijing.

Scientists Discover a Hidden Link Between Cholesterol and Psoriasis

The researchers identified unusually high levels of enzymes called Vanins in dendritic cells from people with psoriasis and several other autoimmune diseases. These enzymes help regulate the processing of certain substances involved in cellular metabolism.

When the scientists reduced Vanin levels, dendritic cells became less active and were less capable of stimulating T cells. They also found that a drug designed to inhibit Vanins prevented psoriasis from developing in mice.

Further investigation revealed why these enzymes might play such an important role.

Vanins convert pantethine into vitamin B5, an essential nutrient that cells need to produce energy. Pantethine is already sold as a nutritional supplement and is commonly used to help lower blood cholesterol because it can reduce cholesterol production.

This connection is particularly interesting because cholesterol does more than circulate in the bloodstream. It also influences how immune cells function. Previous research has shown that cholesterol can stimulate dendritic cell activity, while elevated blood cholesterol is a major risk factor for developing psoriasis.

The team discovered that excessive Vanin activity reduces the amount of pantethine available inside dendritic cells. As pantethine levels fall, cholesterol production increases, causing these immune cells to become unusually active.

Restoring pantethine levels interrupted this process. The supplement reduced cholesterol accumulation within dendritic cells and helped suppress the excessive immune activation associated with inflammation.

"We found that pantethine administration effectively alleviated psoriasis in mice, suggesting that insufficient pantethine levels may be the crucial contributor to hyperactivation of dendritic cells and autoimmune inflammation following the up-regulation of Vanins," Zhang says.

Common Supplement Shows Promise in Human Psoriasis Trial

Encouraged by the laboratory and animal findings, the researchers investigated whether pantethine might also benefit people living with psoriasis.

They conducted a small clinical trial involving 24 patients with the condition. All participants received a topical ointment containing calcipotriene/betamethasone, a combination treatment used to control psoriasis symptoms. Calcipotriene is a vitamin D derivative that helps regulate skin cell growth, while betamethasone is a corticosteroid that reduces inflammation.

Half of the participants also took pantethine tablets, allowing researchers to examine whether adding the supplement improved the results of standard treatment.

After 12 weeks, the patients who received pantethine alongside their prescribed ointment showed greater improvement in psoriasis symptoms. The benefits were especially noticeable among participants who had high blood cholesterol levels before treatment.

These findings suggest that pantethine could potentially serve as an additional treatment for psoriasis, particularly in patients whose cholesterol metabolism may be contributing to inflammation.

However, the trial included only 24 people, and the researchers emphasize that larger studies are necessary to confirm the supplement's effectiveness. The human results also do not establish that the same biological mechanism observed in laboratory experiments is responsible for the improvement in patients.

"Our investigator-initiated clinical trial demonstrated encouraging therapeutic efficacy of pantethine as an adjunctive therapy in psoriasis, but these findings should be interpreted as proof-of-concept for clinical feasibility rather than direct mechanistic validation," Zhang says. "Overall, our study uncovers the Vanin-pantethine-cholestrol axis as a key metabolic pathway governing dendritic cell activation and provides a foundation for therapeutic strategies targeting several dendritic cell-mediated autoimmune diseases."

Materials provided by Rockefeller University Press. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#4365. Battlefield 6 may have actually done it: beaten Call of Duty

Battlefield 6 sales are setting all kinds of records, but one in particular has long eluded the Battlefield series.

If you’ve been paying any attention to the shooter market these past few months, you won’t be surprised to learn that Battlefield 6 has been an unprecedented success for EA, and the Battlefield series as a whole.

The game managed to sell over 7 million units at launch, climbing to the top of the charts anywhere you look, including setting new series concurrent player records on Steam. Thanks to new data, we now better understand the true scale of this launch.

The latest Circana report, which looks at game and hardware sales in the United States, has arrived. This iteration covers the month of October, which is when Battlefield 6 was released.

Battlefield 6 was the top-selling game across all platforms during October - which isn’t surprising. It has overtaken NBA 2K26 to become 2025’s best-selling game year-to-date, making it the best-selling Battlefield game ever.

In October alone, the game sold more than the lifetime sales of Battlefield 1, previously the best-selling entry in the franchise.

Battlefield 6 even set records beyond just its own series, having now produced the highest single-month dollar sales (physical and digital) total for any full game released in the last three years. The previous record holder was 2022’s Modern Warfare 2.

November’s report, which is set to arrive midway through December, will show, once and for all, whether Battlefield 6 has been able to overtake Black Ops 7. With one exception, Call of Duty games have, for more than a decade, topped the best-selling year-to-date chart. Regardless of the quality of the individual titles, or the competition in any given year, nothing has been able to shake that dominance.

Given all this momentum, Battlefield 6 has a shot at dethroning Call of Duty this year, beating Black Ops 7 to become the year’s best-seller. You never want to count out the sheer popularity of Call of Duty among casual players, however, which is what’s going to make December’s report all the more interesting.

#4363. Global fossil fuel emissions set to fall in 2026, but total CO2 keeps rising

Global carbon dioxide emissions from fossil fuels are expected to decline slightly in 2026, offering a promising sign that the world's transition to cleaner energy is beginning to make a measurable difference. According to the latest Global Carbon Budget from the Global Carbon Project, fossil fuel CO2 emissions are projected to fall by 0.4%, partly because of growing solar and wind power generation and disruptions linked to the Iran conflict.

The report estimates that fossil fuel emissions will total 38.2 billion metric tons of carbon dioxide (CO2) in 2026. Oil emissions alone are expected to drop by 1.9%, largely reflecting a temporary energy shock associated with the conflict.

Clean energy is also playing an increasingly important role. Although worldwide energy consumption continues to grow, solar power, wind power, and electric vehicles are now meeting roughly two-thirds of the additional demand. Even so, researchers caution that the transition is not happening quickly enough to guarantee a lasting reduction in fossil fuel emissions.

Fossil Fuel Emissions Fall, but Total CO2 Keeps Rising

Despite the projected decline in fossil fuel emissions, the overall picture is more troubling. When emissions from land-use change (such as deforestation) are included, total global CO2 emissions are expected to reach 43.3 billion metric tons in 2026, compared with 42.8 billion metric tons in 2025.

That increase highlights how progress in cleaner energy can be undermined by continued forest loss and other changes to the landscape.

The report also delivers a stark warning about the world's remaining carbon budget (the amount of CO2 that can be emitted before warming reaches 1.5°C above pre-industrial levels). Researchers estimate that just 150 billion metric tons remain, enough for less than four years at today's emission rates.

As carbon dioxide continues accumulating in the atmosphere, the risks and damaging consequences of climate change are becoming more severe.

Natural Carbon Sinks Face New Climate Pressures

Beyond tracking emissions, the researchers examined the planet's natural "sinks" (absorption of CO2 by land and ocean). These natural systems help limit atmospheric carbon dioxide by taking up some of what human activities release.

The amount of carbon absorbed by land ecosystems has recovered to earlier levels after weakening substantially during the 2023-24 El Niño weather pattern. However, scientists expect the powerful 2026 El Niño to significantly influence carbon absorption in the coming year.

The research brought together experts from the University of Exeter, the University of East Anglia (UEA), the CICERO Center for International Climate Research, Ludwig-Maximilian-University Munich (LMU), the Alfred-Wegener-Institut, and more than 90 additional institutions worldwide.

Professor Pierre Friedlingstein, who directs the Global Carbon Budget Office at the University of Exeter and led the research, emphasized that a temporary reduction in emissions is not enough.

"A decline in fossil CO2 emissions is encouraging, but a reduction driven partly by geopolitical shocks is not a sustainable climate solution."

"The long-term answer remains the rapid deployment of clean energy technologies. While renewables and electric vehicles are increasingly offsetting growth in energy demand, further acceleration is needed if global emissions are to peak and enter a sustained decline."

Clean Energy Could Bring a Historic Turning Point

Despite the challenges, researchers see growing evidence that renewable energy and electric transportation are beginning to change the trajectory of global emissions.

Professor Corinne Le Quéré, Royal Society Research Professor at UEA's School of Environmental Sciences, pointed to the expanding influence of clean technologies, particularly in China.

"Clean technologies are making a real difference in reducing global emissions. Solar and wind power and electric vehicles are expanding rapidly, led by China. Countries on every continent are decreasing their emissions while growing their economies. A further acceleration could turn the tide on global emissions within a few years."

However, a single year of falling emissions does not necessarily mean the world has reached a lasting peak. Glen Peters, Research Professor at the CICERO Center for International Climate Research, stressed the importance of changes that permanently reduce reliance on fossil fuels.

"A drop in emissions in one year is not a peak unless it is driven by structural change. Accelerated deployment of solar, wind, batteries, and electric vehicles is pushing emissions down in dozens of countries and slowing emissions growth in many more, but the changes are not sufficient to lock in a peak in global emissions."

Researchers also emphasize that reducing emissions alone will not be sufficient. Removing carbon dioxide from the atmosphere must become a much larger part of climate strategies.

Professor Julia Pongratz of LMU's Department of Geography explained the challenge:

"Alongside reducing emissions, we need to scale up CO2 removal to reach greenhouse gas neutrality. Afforestation and reforestation already remove substantial amounts of CO2, but these gains are still more than offset by emissions from deforestation, and novel carbon removal remains very limited. We need to act on all these fronts now."

Carbon Emissions in China, the US, India, and Europe

The 2026 Global Carbon Budget reveals significant differences in how emissions are changing across major economies.

China, which accounts for approximately 32% of the world's fossil fuel emissions, is expected to record a 0.9% reduction in 2026 after two consecutive years of relatively slow emissions growth. A substantial decline in oil emissions is helping drive the decrease, although emissions from coal are projected to rise slightly by 0.3%.

At the same time, China continues rapidly expanding electricity generation from renewable sources. The country leads the world in deploying clean technologies and expanding carbon absorption through reforestation. About half of the emissions avoided globally through renewable energy and electric vehicles can be attributed to China. It also has the largest carbon uptake from reforestation and afforestation (new forests).

The United States is projected to reduce emissions by 1.3%, primarily because of lower coal use. Coal emissions increased in 2025 as elevated natural gas prices and cold weather encouraged greater reliance on coal.

India is moving in the opposite direction. Its fossil fuel emissions are expected to grow by 4.4% in 2026, exceeding its average annual growth rate of 3.5% over the past decade.

Elsewhere, the European Union is projected to cut emissions by 1.5%, while Japan is expected to record a 1% reduction.

Taken together, countries outside these major economies are forecast to reduce emissions by 0.7%. Much of that decrease comes from lower oil consumption, likely reflecting higher prices and restrictions on global supplies.

Oil Emissions Decline as Coal Continues to Rise

The report also provides a breakdown of projected emissions from individual fossil fuels.

Oil is expected to experience the largest reduction, with emissions falling 1.9% in 2026. Natural gas emissions are projected to decrease by 0.3%, while coal emissions are expected to increase by 0.6%.

International transportation is also contributing to the overall decline. Emissions from international aviation and international shipping are each forecast to fall by 1%. Reduced aviation activity in the Middle East is partly responsible for the decrease in air travel emissions.

Although these developments help slow fossil fuel emissions, the report indicates that much of the progress remains vulnerable to economic and geopolitical changes.

Deforestation Threatens Global Climate Progress

One of the report's most concerning findings involves carbon emissions from changes in land use.

Although emissions from land-use change have generally declined over the past decade, they are expected to increase to 5.1 billion metric tons of CO2 in 2026.

The projected rise is linked to increased peat fires (almost entirely ignited by human activities) and the degradation of forests in Southeast Asia. Drier conditions associated with the developing El Niño have contributed to these problems.

Even with the latest increase, the long-term growth of total emissions has slowed considerably. Over the past decade, combined emissions from fossil fuels and land-use change increased by an average of 0.3% annually (0.3% per year), compared with 1.7% annually during the preceding decade (1.7% per year).

Permanent deforestation remains a major source of carbon dioxide. Between 2016 and 2025, it released approximately 3.8 billion metric tons of CO2 each year. Reforestation and the establishment of new forests remove substantial amounts of carbon, but these activities offset only about half the emissions associated with permanent deforestation.

China, the 27 countries of the European Union, and the United States together account for the largest carbon removals through reforestation and afforestation, absorbing approximately 0.8 billion metric tons of CO2 annually.

Brazil, Russia, and Indonesia also absorb considerable carbon through forest growth and restoration. However, in those countries, emissions from deforestation outweigh the benefits.

Emerging technologies designed to remove carbon dioxide directly from the atmosphere or through other new approaches are making only a tiny contribution. At their current scale, these methods (excluding conventional means such as reforestation) compensate for less than 30 minutes of annual fossil fuel CO2 emissions.

Meanwhile, the atmospheric concentration of carbon dioxide is projected to reach 427.7 parts per million in 2026, approximately 54% higher than before the Industrial Revolution.

More Countries Are Growing Their Economies While Cutting Emissions

A separate analysis by the same researchers, currently in press in another peer-reviewed journal, offers additional evidence that the expansion of clean energy is changing the relationship between economic growth and carbon emissions.

As global energy demand increases, solar power, wind power, and electric vehicles can prevent some of that additional consumption from producing new fossil fuel emissions (or "offset").

Looking ahead through the end of 2028, the researchers estimate that expanding clean technologies will offset between 64% and 79% of the emissions that would otherwise result from growing energy demand.

Another encouraging trend is the increasing number of countries reducing emissions while their economies continue to expand.

According to the analysis, 59 countries had lower emissions in 2025 than in 2019, before the COVID-19 pandemic, even as their economies grew.

The benefits are not limited to countries where emissions have already begun declining. Between 2019 and 2025, every major world region experienced slower emissions growth, including China, India, and other emerging economies where total emissions continued to rise.

Solar, Wind, and Electric Vehicles Are Reshaping Emissions

Electric vehicles are making an increasingly important contribution to reducing emissions, although their overall impact is still limited by the time required to replace existing gasoline and diesel vehicles.

In 2025, approximately 10% of the global car fleet was electrified (or 6% excluding hybrids). As more conventional vehicles are replaced, electric transportation is expected to play a larger role in reducing fossil fuel consumption.

Solar and wind power are already producing much more substantial benefits.

In 2010, these renewable energy sources prevented an estimated 0.28 billion metric tons of CO2 emissions. By 2025, that figure had climbed to 4.1 billion metric tons, and it is projected to reach 4.6 billion metric tons in 2026.

The sharp increase demonstrates how quickly cleaner electricity generation is expanding and how much additional pollution would be produced without it.

The researchers believe that continued progress could bring the world to a critical milestone sooner than many might expect.

"If further acceleration of clean technology deployment can be supported through time, a sustained peak and decline in global CO2 emissions could be a few years away."

The Global Carbon Budget is compiled annually by an international collaboration of more than 140 scientists. It provides a transparent assessment of global carbon emissions using established scientific methods and undergoes peer review.

The 2026 edition (the 21st annual report) is scheduled for publication as a preprint in Earth System Science Data on November 10, with a peer-reviewed version to follow.

Materials provided by University of Exeter. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#4362. PUBG's extraction shooter spin-off, Black Budget, is finally going to be playable next month

The most interesting development in the PUBG universe, PUBG: Black Budget, is almost ready to show itself off to a wider group of players.

You’d be forgiven for not remembering PUBG: Black Budget, the extraction off-shoot of the original battle royale shooter, PUBG. Black Budget has been sort of floating around the internet for months, but Krafton never really committed to revealing core details about the game, or when players will actually get to play it.

This changes today, as the publisher - along with the game’s developer, PUBG Studios, have finally lifted the lid off the upcoming shooter.

Black Budget is described as a “tactical” extraction shooter. Squads of players infiltrate a mysterious island trapped in a time loop. There’s a bit of a STALKER element here with anomalies and various, unpredictable environmental shifts.

Coli, the island in question, hides a research facility that holds secrets and artefacts, which is what players will be attempting to extract. This is very much a PvPvE shooter, though PUBG Studios says the focus will be on exploration and discovery, rather than constant combat.

The game’s first set of closed alpha tests is set for December. The first takes place December 12-14, and another is scheduled for December 19-21. That’s six days across two weeks, with the test only being available on PC. Both sessions will be open to players in North America, Europe, and Asia.

As it usually works with these sorts of tets on Steam, the game’s Steam page has a link where you can request access. If granted, you’ll be able to find the closed alpha in your library and download it when the time comes.

Though this is a closed test, Krafton confirmed that players will be able to capture and livestream their gameplay. In fact, watching content creators might be how you get access, as Black Budget is going to have a Twitch Drops event running alongside those sessions.

When I played Arc Raiders prior to its launch, I likened its tense and uncertain atmosphere to that of the early days of PUBG, so it’s going to be very interesting to see what actual PUBG does with the extraction shooter premise.

So far, it sounds like it’s going to be doing its own thing, leaning more into the adventure side of the subgenre, but we’ll have to see how it all shakes out when the tests start. Indeed, the BR-like constantly shrinking circle sounds like it could be a game-changing twist.

#4361. Interview: Trophy Games CEO Søren Gleie on 20 years of mobile game development, the role of AI, and dream projects

Founded in 2006, Trophy Games has spent two decades establishing itself as a recognised name in mobile gaming, putting its own unique stamp on the management simulation genre with the release of its debut football management sim, Trophy Manager.

And, while Trophy Games would later return to football management with Pro 11 and Women's Soccer Manager, its ambitions didn't stop at the beautiful game.

Its subsequent ventures into the world of transport has laid new ground for success, with Truck Manager becoming a particular fan favourite. Packed with the appeal of expanding your workforce, keeping pace with the competition and strategising to keep the profits ticking over, it's another example of Trophy Games' knack for developing deep management experiences traditionally associated with PC and browser-based gaming.

So, what's next for the studio? Well, we caught up with Søren Gleie, CEO of Trophy Games, to find out what the future holds for the developer. As a little teaser, the possibilities could span new ventures in fishing, airport management and theme parks, as well as the less explored but fertile (excuse the pun) world of horse breeding.

Søren Gleie, CEO of Trophy Games. Photo provided courtesy of Trophy Games. Could you tell us a bit about yourself and how you first got into the games industry? I have always made games, including non-computer games, with my childhood friend Niklas.

We eventually decided to make a football game, bicycled to the library to borrow books about programming, and went on to create Trophy Games in 2006, starting with our original browser-based title, Trophy Manager.

This has been my first and only games industry experience. Over the past two decades, Trophy Games has grown into a publicly traded studio on Nasdaq First North Copenhagen, expanding our focus onto mobile and PC live-service games while reaching over 100 million total installs. Trophy Games celebrated its 20th anniversary this year, which is a remarkable achievement. What have been some of the biggest challenges along the way, and which personal achievements are you most proud of? The first ten years of Trophy Games history we were balancing on bankruptcy every month while at the same time putting out fires both in game code and server setup. I don’t miss that period. On the achievement side, I am immensely proud of reaching our 20-year milestone and growing the company every single year since 2006.

On top of that, a key testament to our strong culture is that our first 5 employees are still with us today as we continue to find our space, learn new things, and constantly strive to improve. Your portfolio of management games spans trucking, railways, aviation, farming, energy and shipping. Are there other industries you’d like to explore next? We are always exploring new offline passions and real-world simulation themes where we can apply our proven Transport series framework. Most recently, we launched Space Manager, and we are currently exploring concepts around horse breeding and fishing simulation games.

Additionally, with our acquisition of Playrion, we aim to use titles like Airport Simulator as a foundation for a new series of tycoon simulation games; it could go towards hospitals, pets, theme parks or something entirely different.

Vehicle management sims usually tend to dominate the mobile space, yet Truck Manager and Farm Manager have both found particular appeal as management titles. What do you think has been the key to their success? I think there’s a good market for less action-packed games with shorter sessions. Many adults are passionate about games but struggle to find the time to dedicate to it. So instead, being able to build something and be good at it within 10 minute sessions is a nice compromise. The key for us lies in offering deep, authentic real-world simulation mechanics combined with an accessible free-to-play live-service structure on mobile and PC. With AI tools increasingly being used in game development, where do you see the greatest opportunities for it with a studio like Trophy Games, and what potential pitfalls do you think developers need to be wary of? What we see now is a huge influx of casual and hypercasual games. A sort of revival. For Trophy Games, the impact is an increased focus on longevity and, as a consequence, higher lifetime value that will allow our performance marketing to stay ahead of the competition. AI presents huge opportunities in streamlining content creation, reducing development timelines, and enabling us to efficiently iterate and scale our modular game structures across new genres.

However, the main pitfall is that AI accelerates whatever strategy you give it — it amplifies good execution but won’t save a weak concept, so developers must remain focused on clear target audiences and strong game design, rather than relying on AI to fix underlying product issues. Looking ahead, where do you see Trophy Games in the next five years, and what would you most like the studio to achieve during that time? Hopefully we will be able to celebrate 25 years of consecutive growth. I see Trophy Games continuing to consolidate its position as a leading global developer and publisher of free-to-play simulation and management games. I would love to see us successfully expand our formula into new tycoon genres, continue executing strategic mergers & acquisitions to revitalize acquired titles, and deliver strong profits while keeping millions of players engaged across our portfolio. If budget and development time were no object, what would your dream project look like? If budget and development time were unlimited, my dream project would be an ultra-detailed, interconnected global logistics and management ecosystem. It would seamlessly combine air, land, sea, and space transportation networks with deep economic simulation, allowing players

to build and manage multi-modal global transport empires with real-time multiplayer dynamics, like co-op or competition.

Here’s to the future! As you can see, there's plenty to look forward to in this next chapter for Trophy Games, with even more for its fans to get excited about. With new titles on the horizon, we suggest you visit the Trophy Games website and explore some of the studio's existing classics. All are free-to-play, offering plenty of challenges and unique rewards and experiences to discover.

#4360. Obesity linked to up to 27% lower risk of death in dementia

A surprising new study has found that people who are overweight or obese when diagnosed with dementia tend to live longer than those who have a normal body weight. The findings challenge expectations about the relationship between weight and health, suggesting that carrying extra weight may be associated with an unexpected survival advantage after dementia develops.

Researchers from Columbia University Mailman School of Public Health and NYU School of Global Public Health found that body weight at the time of diagnosis may provide important clues about how long someone with dementia is likely to live. Their findings, published in the Journal of Alzheimer's Disease, also highlight the importance of proper nutrition for people living with the condition.

The results are particularly intriguing because obesity is well established as a risk factor for several serious health problems, including heart disease and diabetes. Being overweight or obese during middle age is also associated with a greater likelihood of developing dementia later in life. However, previous research has suggested that the relationship may reverse once dementia has developed, with higher body weight linked to better survival.

"Because this finding is somewhat counterintuitive, an important question is whether it could simply be an artifact of bias. Our analyses suggest that the major sources of bias we examined do not explain the survival advantage associated with higher weight," said corresponding author Yuan Zhang, PhD, assistant professor of Sociomedical Sciences at Columbia Mailman and in the Butler Columbia Aging Center.

Obesity Linked to Up to 27% Lower Risk of Death

The researchers found substantial differences in survival based on body weight at the time of dementia diagnosis. Compared with individuals in the normal weight range, those who were overweight or obese had a significantly lower risk of death, even after the researchers accounted for smoking, existing medical conditions, and demographic characteristics.

People classified as overweight (body mass index of 25 to 29.9) had a 16 percent lower risk of death. Those with class 1 obesity (BMI of 30 to 34.9) had an even larger reduction of 27 percent, while individuals with class 2 and 3 obesity (BMI equal to or greater than 35) had a 22 percent lower risk.

Despite these striking differences, the researchers caution that the findings should not be interpreted as a recommendation for people with dementia to gain weight.

"This doesn't mean that patients with dementia should attempt to become overweight or obese, as our study was not designed to test that question. But our findings do suggest that weight status may serve as a useful prognostic signal for survival at the time of dementia diagnosis. They also support the notion that nutrition is a key factor in the health and survival of people with dementia," said Virginia Chang, associate professor of Social and Behavioral Sciences at NYU School of Global Public Health and the study's first author.

Tracking Weight and Dementia Over 24 Years

To investigate the connection, Zhang, Chang, and their colleagues examined information from the Health and Retirement Study, a nationally representative research project that follows Americans ages 51 and older.

The team analyzed records collected between 1998 and 2022, focusing on 4,523 participants who did not have dementia when they entered the study but subsequently developed the condition.

Because the data covered such a long period, the researchers could examine how participants' weight changed in the years leading up to their diagnosis. They could also determine their weight when dementia was identified and track their survival afterward.

This extended timeline was especially important because scientists have questioned whether the apparent benefit of higher body weight is genuine or simply reflects misleading patterns in the data. One possibility is that having additional fat or muscle gives patients resources that help them withstand the physical effects of dementia. Another is that the association arises from factors that earlier studies did not adequately consider.

Could Weight Loss Explain the Dementia Paradox?

One major concern involves weight loss that occurs before dementia becomes clinically apparent.

Earlier research by Zhang and Chang found that people can begin losing weight as much as 10 years before a dementia diagnosis, with the decline becoming more pronounced as the disease approaches.

This creates a potential problem for studies that measure weight only at the time dementia is diagnosed. Some individuals classified as having a normal weight may previously have been heavier and lost weight because of the developing disease. If those individuals are already experiencing more advanced illness, they may face a greater risk of death, making higher body weight appear beneficial by comparison.

The researchers also considered other possible distortions. Restricting an analysis to people who develop dementia can create misleading relationships between obesity and mortality, even when the underlying connection is more complicated.

Another concern is known as "survivor" bias. Since people with obesity face an increased risk of dying from certain illnesses before reaching the age when dementia typically develops, those who survive long enough to receive a dementia diagnosis may represent an unusually healthy group.

To determine whether these factors explained the findings, the team performed additional analyses designed to evaluate several potential sources of bias. The results indicated that the biases they examined were unlikely to be major drivers of the observed connection between higher weight and lower mortality.

Why Extra Weight Might Help People With Dementia

Although the precise explanation remains unknown, the researchers identified several biological reasons why additional body weight could be advantageous for someone already living with dementia.

One possibility involves the body's energy reserves. People with more stored fat or greater muscle mass may be better equipped to withstand periods of poor nutrition and the physical deterioration that can accompany the disease.

Dementia can interfere with eating in several ways. Changes in brain function may reduce appetite or motivation to eat, while some patients experience increased energy needs or gradually lose the ability to feed themselves. Over time, these problems can contribute to significant weight loss, muscle wasting, and declining health.

"Nutrition can be a big problem for people with dementia," said Chang. "They may experience wasting and an inability to eat, which can be due to changes in the brain's central drive, leading to loss of appetite and initiative, increased energy expenditure, and difficulties feeding themselves."

Having additional energy stores or muscle tissue could potentially help patients cope with these challenges, although the study did not establish that these factors directly explain the survival differences.

The researchers emphasize that important questions remain unanswered. Even after examining multiple potential biases and identifying plausible biological explanations, they cannot say for certain why overweight and obese participants experienced lower mortality.

Nevertheless, Zhang and Chang believe that weight at the time of a dementia diagnosis could provide valuable information about a patient's likely survival. The results also reinforce the importance of recognizing and addressing nutritional problems in people with dementia.

Additional study authors include Eleanor Hayes-Larson of the University of Southern California and Hui Zheng of the University of Toronto.

The research received funding from the National Institutes of Health (grant numbers R00AG070274, R00AG075317).

#4359. An Elder Scrolls Classic Is Finally Getting the Remaster It Deserves After 22 Years

Covering the video games industry since 2017, with experience in news, articles, and reviews. Currently a writer at DualShockers and gaming magazines.

As a nostalgic gamer, I have a soft spot for forgotten games that were left behind by time, especially when they're part of a franchise as beloved as The Elder Scrolls.

While most players have spent the past two decades exploring Morrowind, Oblivion, and Skyrim, one rather unusual entry in the series has been sitting on a much less familiar platform: the Nokia N-Gage. Thankfully, that's about to change!

The Elder Scrolls Travels: Shadowkey, a first-person RPG originally released in 2004, is getting a second chance thanks to an independent project called Shadowkey Reforged.

Developed by Dan Whelan, the project brings the forgotten spin-off to Windows, Mac, and Android with a new engine, widescreen support, controller compatibility, and plenty of visual and gameplay improvements. Even better, it's launching today, November 11.

Morrowind is rightfully regarded as one of the greatest open-world RPGs of all time, but it's aged badly and would benefit from a full remake.

For anyone unfamiliar with it, Shadowkey was the third entry in The Elder Scrolls Travels, a series of portable spin-offs released between Morrowind and Oblivion. Unlike the mainline games, however, it was exclusive to Nokia's N-Gage, a rather ambitious handheld-phone hybrid that didn't exactly have the longest life on the market.

That exclusivity made Shadowkey one of the more inaccessible chapters in the franchise's history. And while you could technically track down the original hardware and a copy of the game, that's hardly the most convenient way to revisit a 22-year-old RPG.

That's where Shadowkey Reforged comes in! Rather than simply emulating the N-Gage, Whelan built a new engine capable of running the original game's data and scripts on modern devices. Players can choose between a Classic mode that preserves the original presentation and a Modern mode featuring upgraded artwork, improved lighting, and several gameplay additions. So yes, it is literally the best of both worlds.

For anyone unfamiliar with it, Shadowkey was the third entry in The Elder Scrolls Travels, a series of portable spin-offs released between Morrowind and Oblivion.

The latter isn't just a fresh coat of paint, by the way. Modern mode introduces features inspired by newer Elder Scrolls games, including stamina-based sprinting, stealth, and ragdoll physics. You can also toggle individual features to customize the experience instead of committing to one preset. And if you happen to have The Elder Scrolls III: Morrowind installed, there's another neat little bonus: Shadowkey Reforged can use its soundtrack and sound effects, preserving a connection between two games released during the same era, in case you want an extra touch!

Skyblivion team says a former volunteer is threatening legal action, even after the devs removed their code and rebuilt the affected systems.

Interestingly, Whelan has also been transparent about using AI during development. According to the developer, AI tools helped with coding, building the engine, and debugging, while the updated artwork combines AI-generated images with Photoshop and manual sprite editing.

Shadowkey Reforged is available as a free, unofficial project, with versions for Windows, Mac, and Android. However, there's one important detail players should know before getting too excited: the download doesn't include the original game's files. This means you'll need to provide your own copy of Shadowkey to play it – you can check more info about that on the port’s website.

Still, it's great to see such an obscure piece of The Elder Scrolls history getting another shot at life. Bethesda hasn't announced an official remaster, but Whelan's project might be the closest many players will get to experiencing this forgotten adventure without digging up a Nokia N-Gage.

#4357. Dragon boy Durin is the star of the show in Genshin Impact's wintry Luna 3 update, launching in early December

Genshin Impact is getting two new characters and a whole host of new content in Version Luna 3, which arrives in under two weeks.

The latest HoYoverse Special Program has brought us big Genshin Impact news. Version Luna 3 has been fully revealed, continuing the Nod-Krai story. The new chapter arrives December 3 across all platforms.

The Moon-Prayer Night is the big in-world festival, marking Dameselette's final night before she sets off for the moon. The new update, of course, introduces new playable characters, one with an interesting mechanic.

The events of this new chapter take place following Rarcher of Solnari’s defeat. The victory has given way to the Moon-Prayer Night celebrations, which brings various stalls to the Nasha Town, alongside a new souvenir stamp book where you can record your memories.

All is not fine, however, as Alice and Nicole Reeyn come bearing some bad news about phantoms appearing across the Nod-Krai region at Teyvat's borders. There’s a mystery to be uncovered here, and your journey to do so won’t be a lonely one.

The highly-anticipated Durin is at last the new playable character. A 5-Star Pyro Sword wielder, Durin can switch between two different forms: one lets him deal damage, while the other is best suited to supporting the team.

Durin was once a dragon, you see, who was later given a human body. This is why he’s able to switch forms. The more powerful, Abyssal-infused form can launch major attacks on single targets to boost his own Vaporize and Melt damage, while his support form reduces enemies’ Elemental Resistance and deals AoE Pyro damage.

Durin’s Story Quest will shed more light on that aspect of his life, and completing it earns you a reward for him. Speaking of quests, completing the Archon Quest will grant you 500 Primogems. As a member of Hexenzirkel, Durin and other characters can gain new powers when you complete more quests in Moon-Prayer Night.

All characters connected to the Hexenzirkel can benefit from certain story quests tied to their abilities. This is a big new addition, and will affect Venti, Klee, Albedo, Mona, Razor, Fischl, and Sucrose - all of whom can become Hexerei characters. This ties into the new Hexerei Secret Rite effect, which will trigger when two or more Hexerei characters are present. The effect boosts the entire party’s combat effectiveness.

The other new character in Luna 3 is Jahoda, a 4-Star Anemo Bow wielder who’s great at healing teammates and absorbing Elements, which she can then use to deal damage. The first phase of Luna 3 will feature Durin and Jahoda, alongside the return of Venti. The second phase sees no new character debuts, but does feature the return of Varesa and Xilonen.

There’s more to get excited about in Luna 3, even if you don’t feel like spending most of your time in Nod-Krai. #4356. NASA offers $500,000 to develop next-generation electric rocket engines

NASA is offering $500,000 in prizes to encourage American companies to develop more capable electric propulsion systems for future space missions. The competition focuses on a technology known as Hall effect thrusters, which use electricity to propel spacecraft through space.

The new initiative, called the Advanced Mid-Power Electric Rocket (AMPERE) Challenge, seeks to advance mid-power (3-7 kW) propulsion systems. Government agencies and aerospace industry experts have identified this class of thrusters as an important technology for satellite operations, national defense, and space exploration.

By inviting commercial companies to design and demonstrate working prototypes, NASA hopes to accelerate progress in electric propulsion and help prepare promising technologies for practical use.

Unlike conventional rockets, which burn chemical propellants to produce powerful bursts of thrust, electric propulsion systems use electrical energy to accelerate charged particles and expel them at high speeds. The resulting force pushes a spacecraft in the opposite direction.

Hall effect thrusters are a particular type of electric propulsion system that uses electric and magnetic fields to control and accelerate charged particles. They typically produce much less thrust than chemical rocket engines, but they can use propellant far more efficiently.

That efficiency makes electric thrusters especially valuable for missions that require spacecraft to operate for extended periods. Rather than delivering a brief, powerful push, these engines can provide gentle acceleration over long stretches of time, gradually changing a spacecraft's speed or trajectory.

Hall effect thrusters are already used in space, including for adjusting satellite orbits and maintaining spacecraft positions. Improving their performance could expand the range of missions they can support.

The power range targeted by NASA's challenge refers to the electrical energy these systems consume. A kilowatt equals 1,000 watts, so the competition focuses on thrusters that operate using approximately 3,000 to 7,000 watts of electrical power.

NASA Seeks More Advanced Spacecraft Thrusters

The AMPERE Challenge is designed to help American companies move promising electric propulsion concepts beyond early development and toward technologies that can be evaluated under realistic testing conditions.

Participating companies will develop and demonstrate Hall-effect thruster prototypes within the specified power range. NASA intends to assess their performance using its testing facilities, providing an opportunity to evaluate how well the systems function and identify areas that need improvement.

This testing is an important step in turning experimental propulsion technology into equipment suitable for future missions. Spacecraft engines must deliver predictable performance and operate reliably in the demanding environment of space.

By supporting commercial innovation, NASA aims to strengthen the technological foundation for future government and private sector missions. Potential applications include satellite operations, defense systems, and robotic exploration beyond Earth.

$500,000 in Prizes for Electric Propulsion Innovation

NASA has allocated a total of $500,000 in cash prizes for the AMPERE Challenge. The competition will take place across three phases, with as many as two winning teams eligible to receive up to $250,000 each.

In addition to the financial awards, winning teams can gain access to NASA testing resources and technology. These opportunities could help companies evaluate and improve their propulsion systems while advancing their readiness for future applications.

The challenge is open to commercial companies that are incorporated in the United States and maintain their primary place of business in the country.

Registration begins November 9, 2026, and closes January 27, 2027.

Companies interested in participating can find complete competition rules, eligibility requirements, and registration information on the official NASA AMPERE Challenge website.

Through this competition, NASA hopes to encourage new advances in electric rocket technology and strengthen the propulsion capabilities available for the next generation of spacecraft.

#4354. Pokémon Night Out underlines why Location Backgrounds are fantastic for Pokémon Go fans

Pokémon Go has a lot of specific, in-person events. Things like Into the Wild which is coming up this weekend (which had previous locations in Lisbon) or Go Fest that happens each year. Beyond these location-heavy events, where there are lots of smaller set up, specific installations of Pokémon branding around: We've seen a bunch of lower-key events like the National Trust and Space Centre collaborations. None of these were quite the same as Pokémon Night Out, though.

In a Go Fest or Into the Wild-type event, everything is targeted towards in-game usage; getting players in person, together, for a set amount of time. On the other hand, the National Trust and Space Centre collaborations are long-running,with minimal in-person activities, and real dependence on the app. Pokémon Night Out was something different altogether; there were tons of in-game things to do for people in the area interested in Pokémon Go, but there was also a huge concert for Pokémon fans in general.

I have never considered going to an EDM Concert and really didn't know who Alison Wonderland or Marshmello were, but I was pumped to go along to this! When we entered the O2 in London, we could see loads of people walking around, staying out of the rain, wearing Pokémon clothing. They were raiding, chatting and hanging out! You see, this event space had a really cool postcard that appeared in-game, some research questlines, and tons of raids. These raids included Pikachu and Gengar with a nighttime London background.

They are specifically in-person raids, so many people came to the area to both Raid and pick up these questlines. There was also a merch stand outside the O2, with a less busy one beyond where the tickets were scanned. Going into the actual area beyond ticket scanning had a different vibe. There were some people playing Pokémon Go, but also some Pokémon fans and cosplayers there, excited for this sort of event. Pokémon had set up some photo areas and handed out a tote bag, with a poster and bracelets in it. A lot was going on!

We found our seats quite quickly and were happy with our spot, quickly getting to know our neighbours. One of the most interesting things, however, was that there were so many people playing Pokémon Go - below us on the stairs, next to us, around us. These people were all after a Shiny with the London background. Backgrounds had always been cool, but as Pokémon has added the ability to show off that background around your player's profile, there is even more of a drive to have these less common location backgrounds. Although there were plenty of Raids, this event was less than a day long. Equally interesting was the fact that this was never really listed as a Pokemon Go event, so it was unlikely many of these (hundreds) of players actually booked tickets for this extra layer of gaming.

This really goes hand in hand with what Ed Wu, President, Games at Scopely said to me earlier in the year, "We are trying to inspire people to explore the world together through the magic of making Pokemon real in the real world." Memories are one of the core pillars of Pokemon Go, so knowing that all of the people catching would see that background on their Pikachu and Gengar's in future, surely means that Scopely Explore are already starting to deliver on that pillar.

The show itself was fantastic - such a unique and interesting experience with a Rave Pikachu and Mimikyu coming on stage, with tons of visual effects and nods to retro Pokémon games. This just felt like a big, maybe slightly strange to me, celebration of all things Pokémon. I find it really fun when Pokémon Go is used alongside Pokémon events in this way, feeling like it's part of the drive of what brings people together, without the event being specifically Pokémon Go-themed. I look forward to seeing who on my friends list has backgrounds around their avatar showcasing some of the other EDM locations and who has backgrounds from other events that I have attended, as it helps this already social-friendly game give an extra something to share and discuss.

#4352. Inside this quantum computer, memory vibrates like a guitar string

A quantum computer might seem to have little in common with a guitar, but researchers at ETH Zurich have found a surprising connection. Physicist Yiwen Chu and her team have developed a system that uses microscopic mechanical vibrations to store and manipulate quantum information, much like the vibrating strings of a guitar produce musical notes.

Unlike the sounds produced by a musical instrument, these vibrations occur at frequencies far beyond human hearing. They take place within a tiny quantum chip, where they serve as a new form of computer memory.

By harnessing these vibrations, the researchers have created a way for quantum computers to process information efficiently while accessing a flexible working memory. "The interaction between the quantum processor and the quantum memory provides a crucial foundation with a view to establishing quantum computers as a powerful and reliable way to perform computations that are not feasible with conventional computers," says Yiwen Chu.

The breakthrough, described in the journal Science, introduces a different approach to quantum computer design. Instead of closely integrating information processing and storage, as many existing systems do, Chu's team has developed an architecture that gives these functions more distinct roles.

Quantum Memory Inspired by Conventional Computers

The researchers drew inspiration from the basic design of everyday digital computers. In a conventional machine, the central processing unit (CPU) carries out calculations while information is held separately in working memory, commonly called random access memory (RAM). The arrangement of these components plays an important role in determining how efficiently a computer operates.

Chu's quantum system follows a similar principle. A superconducting qubit acts as the processing and control unit, performing a role comparable to that of the central processing unit (CPU). Meanwhile, a separate quantum memory temporarily holds the information needed during calculations, allowing the processor to retrieve and modify it as necessary.

The major difference lies in how that information is stored.

"In our quantum working memory, however, information is not stored electromagnetically -- as is usually the case today -- but rather in the form of mechanical vibrations," explains Chu.

Quantum computers take advantage of unusual properties of quantum physics, including superposition, which allows quantum systems to exist in combinations of different states, and entanglement, which creates powerful connections between quantum states. These effects could eventually enable quantum machines to tackle certain extremely complicated calculations much faster than conventional computers, including some problems that are currently beyond their practical capabilities.

Why Vibrating Quantum Memory Could Be Better

One of the greatest challenges in quantum computing is maintaining precise control over quantum information. The states used for calculations are delicate, and even small disturbances can cause information to be lost. To perform calculations reliably, the processor and memory must interact closely enough to transfer and manipulate quantum states with high precision.

In the new system, microscopic structures called mechanical resonators hold information in particular patterns of vibration. When the superconducting qubit needs that information, it accesses the stored vibrational state, performs the required operation, and returns the modified information to memory.

Many existing quantum computers instead use electromagnetic memory alongside superconducting qubits. Researchers understand these technologies well, and they can be combined to provide extremely accurate control over quantum states, including reading, changing, and manipulating stored information.

However, electromagnetic memory systems have a significant disadvantage. They can occupy considerable space, making it difficult to expand experimental quantum devices into the larger, more capable computers that researchers and industries ultimately need.

Mechanical resonators offer several potential advantages. They are substantially smaller, allowing more compact designs. They can also support numerous different patterns of vibration, providing opportunities to store more information simultaneously than conventional electromagnetic memory.

Another important benefit is that mechanical vibrations can preserve quantum states for longer periods before the stored information begins to fade. Longer storage times could make it easier to carry out complicated calculations that require information to remain available throughout multiple processing steps.

The research published in Science provides the first experimental demonstration that mechanical resonators can work together with superconducting qubits to carry out quantum computations. The results establish that vibration-based memory is a feasible alternative to electromagnetic storage.

The achievement goes beyond simply storing information. Chu's team demonstrated that its architecture can handle both relatively straightforward calculations and more demanding quantum operations.

To evaluate the system, the researchers tested two important computational techniques: the quantum Fourier transform and period finding. Both are fundamental tools in quantum computing and require a computer to coordinate multiple quantum states with considerable precision.

"The Quantum Fourier Transform is a fundamental computational procedure required for many quantum algorithms. The period-finding algorithm we implemented served as a demonstration of how this procedure can be used," explains Igor Kladaric, doctoral student in Chu's team and co-author of the publication.

Successfully completing these tasks requires the system to store, control, and maintain coherent relationships among multiple quantum states at the same time. The experiments showed that the new architecture can meet these requirements, providing strong evidence that it can support genuine quantum computation rather than simply function as a memory device.

A Promising Step Toward Powerful Quantum Computers

One of the most significant findings is that the new system can, in principle, carry out all the fundamental operations needed for arbitrary quantum computations. This means the architecture has the essential capabilities required for a programmable, general-purpose quantum computer.

However, demonstrating those capabilities in an experimental chip is only the beginning. The next major challenge is scaling the technology to larger systems with greater processing power while preserving the precision and reliability demonstrated in the laboratory.

Chu and her colleagues are continuing to investigate how their approach can be developed further. Its long-term success will depend on whether mechanical quantum memory can remain effective as more components and increasingly complex computations are added.

Practical quantum computers powerful enough for widespread scientific and industrial applications are still some distance away. Nevertheless, by showing that tiny mechanical vibrations can serve as compact, capable quantum memory, the ETH Zurich team has demonstrated a promising new route toward making those machines a reality.

#4349. The Witcher 3 Is Using AI for Geralt’s Voice, But There’s a Very Good Reason

Covering the video games industry since 2017, with experience in news, articles, and reviews. Currently a writer at DualShockers and gaming magazines.

Artificial intelligence has become one of the most controversial topics in the gaming industry, and it's not hard to understand why. From studios experimenting with AI-generated assets to developers finding new ways to automate creative work, players have plenty of reasons to be skeptical.

However, CD Projekt Red has found a rather unusual way to use the technology in The Witcher 3, and this time, there's a surprisingly touching story behind it.

The studio has recently confirmed that it is working with an AI company to adjust Geralt's Polish voice in the upcoming Songs of the Past expansion, which raised some players’ eyebrows. But don't worry, Jacek Rozenek, the actor who has portrayed the White Wolf in Polish since the original The Witcher, isn't being replaced.

In fact, he's still performing all of Geralt's new lines himself. This time, AI is actually being used as a supportive tool and is simply helping his voice sound closer to the one players remember from the 2015 RPG.

Amanita Design, the Czech studio behind Machinarium, recently called out an AI-generated project made using assets from the game.

As reported by Game File, Rozenek suffered a stroke in 2019 that left him unable to speak for months. His recovery was an incredibly difficult process, requiring him to train his voice for six or seven hours every day before he could return to acting.

He eventually returned to the role of Geralt, recording additional lines for The Witcher 3's next-gen update in 2022. However, the process took a significant toll on him. Rozenek told Game File that he was exhausted after those recording sessions, despite having worked hard to regain his ability to perform.

Jacek Rozenek, the actor who has portrayed the White Wolf in Polish since the original The Witcher, isn't being replaced.

When CD Projekt invited him back to record dialogue for Songs of the Past, the studio noticed that his voice had changed considerably. It was now lower and rougher than it had been when he recorded the thousands of lines featured in the original game.

Since the new expansion takes place around the same period as the base game, hearing Geralt suddenly sound different between old and new dialogue could not make sense to the player’s experience. So, rather than replacing Rozenek, however, CD Projekt decided to find another solution. A quite smart one, actually.

The studio partnered with Respeecher, an AI company specializing in voice technology that it had previously worked with on Phantom Liberty, the DLC of Cyberpunk 2077. With their help, Rozenek recorded all of Geralt's new dialogue as usual, and the recordings were then processed using an algorithm trained on his previous performances.

CD Projekt Red has just released Patch 5.01 for The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt Remastered.

In other words, the technology isn't generating Geralt's lines from scratch or replacing the actor's performance. Rozenek still delivers the dialogue, including its emotions and acting, while AI helps bring his voice closer to the version players heard over a decade ago.

Most importantly, the actor gave his full consent to the process and expressed his trust in the developers. "The point is that this voice should be as close as possible to my voice from 12 years ago," Rozenek explained.

CD Projekt's localization producer, Mikołaj Szwed, also acknowledged the concerns surrounding AI in the industry, but believes this is an example of how the technology can be used ethically. He described the situation as a special case, emphasizing that the decision was made because of Rozenek's health circumstances.

And honestly, it's difficult to argue with the sentiment behind it. Rather than using AI to cut costs or avoid hiring a performer, the Polish studio is using it to help an actor continue playing a character he's portrayed for decades. Songs of the Past is currently scheduled to launch in 2027, and Geralt's Polish voice will once again be in the hands of the person who helped make him so iconic!
